chunk_findings.detail: The commit's stated invariant — "A line still too long keeps its first _CMD_SHOWN characters and gains its tail, so nothing shown before is lost" — is false for the tail. Before the change, `tail = _CMD_SHOWN // 3` = 66, so the message ended with the last 66 characters; now it ends with `cmd[-_CMD_TAIL:]` = the last 60. Characters at offsets 61–66 from the end that were previously visible are now inside the elided middle. Concrete input: a holder cmdline whose basenamed form is 300 characters long and whose identifying argument sits 62 characters from the end (e.g. `... <56 chars> --hold dd` — old note contained it via `cmd[-66:]`, new note cuts it because `cmd[-60:]` starts 6 characters later); for the trivial case `cmd = "x"*300` the old note exposed `x` at offset −66..−61 and the new one does not. The test added in the same commit (`test_a_long_command_still_shows_everything_the_old_cut_showed`) only checks a token at offset ~150, i.e. in the head, so it does not protect the tail budget that was silently reduced.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py `_describe_pid` (truncation line, new `cmd = f"{cmd[:_CMD_SHOWN]}...{cmd[-_CMD_TAIL:]}"`)

chunk_findings.detail: Replacing `argv[0].startswith("python")` with `_PYTHON.fullmatch(argv[0])` no longer matches real CPython interpreter basenames that carry a `t`/`d` suffix. Free-threaded builds are installed as `python3.13t` (PEP 703) and debug builds as `python3.13d` / Debian's `python3-dbg`; all of these matched the old `startswith("python")` and fail `fullmatch(r"python[0-9.]*")`. For such a holder the script argument is no longer reduced to its basename, so a long script path is emitted verbatim and eats the `_CMD_SHOWN` head — the exact failure mode this bug is about. Concrete input: `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` = `b"/usr/bin/python3.13t\0/very/long/scratch/path/to/entrypoint.py\0-m\0ddflow.infra.log\0"`; the new code returns `pid <n> (python3.13t /very/long/scratch/path/to/entrypoint.py -m ddflow.infra.log)` (and with a longer path the `ddflow.infra.log` argument is pushed past the 200-char head), whereas the old code produced `python3.13t entrypoint.py ...`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py `_PYTHON = re.compile(r"python[0-9.]*")`

chunk_findings.detail: The new pattern `python[0-9.]*[a-z]?(-dbg)?` only ever accepts **one** trailing ABI-suffix letter, but CPython's ABI flags compose: a build configured with both free-threading (`--disable-gil`, suffix `t`) and `--with-pydebug` (suffix `d`) installs its interpreter as `python3.13td` (or `python3.13dt`, depending on flag ordering). `_PYTHON.fullmatch("python3.13td")` returns `None`: `[0-9.]*` consumes `3.13`, `[a-z]?` consumes one letter, and the second suffix letter is left over (the `(-dbg)?` group cannot absorb it). Since `_describe_pid` only takes the "names its script" branch for a recognized interpreter, such a process falls into the fallback that shows the raw argv, so for a cmdline like `/long/scratch/.../venv/bin/python3.13td\0-m\0ddflow.infra.log\0...` the 200-char head (`_CMD_SHOWN`) is still entirely the long interpreter path and the identifying `ddflow.infra.log` part is still cut off — i.e. bug B3a4bf051b4 reproduces verbatim on exactly the "build-suffixed interpreter" class this hunk claims to fix. The added regression test cannot catch this because it only parametrizes the single-suffix names `python3.13t`, `python3.13d`, `python3-dbg`, `python`, and uses a short `/usr/bin/...` path.

chunk_findings.detail: `upstream_offer` resolves `BUG_REPORT_COMMAND` as a global of `ddflow.api.knowledge.bugs`. While this code lived in `ddflow/api/knowledge.py`, the module the function read the constant from was the same module object the package path `ddflow.api.knowledge` referred to, so a test/caller doing `ddflow.api.knowledge.BUG_REPORT_COMMAND = "ddflow bug report {id}"` (or monkeypatching `ddflow.api.knowledge.upstream_offer` to a stub, since `bug_found` calls the bs module global) changed what `upstream_offer` / `bug_found` observed. After the move those are two different namespaces: the package `__init__` only re-exports a *copy* of the string, and rebinding `ddflow.api.knowledge.BUG_REPORT_COMMAND` leaves `bugs.BUG_REPORT_COMMAND` at `""`, so `upstream_offer` returns `""` and the offer is silently dropped. The in-file comment points at `tests/test_bug_scope.py` as the consumer of this constant, so any test (or caller, e.g. the bug-report command wiring) that sets it through the old module path now exercises a value the moved function never reads. Callers/tests must patch `ddflow.api.knowledge.bugs.BUG_REPORT_COMMAND` (and `...bugs.upstream_offer`) instead, or the package must proxy attribute access rather than re-export by value.

chunk_findings.detail:
`claims_fix` is built as

```python
rf"\bfix(?:es|ed|ing)?\s+(?:bugs?\s+)?(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*(?:and\s+)?"
rf"{re.escape(bug.id)}(?![\w-])"
```

Inside the repeated list group `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*` the comma is **mandatory** for every consumed element, and the id is only tried after that group and after an optional `(?:and\s+)?`. So the element joined by "and" is never reachable whenever anything precedes it: the group can consume `B29, ` but cannot consume `B31 ` (no trailing comma), so the cursor is left on `B31`, `(?:and\s+)?` fails to match `and`, and `B30` is compared against `B31`. Backtracking the group to zero iterations leaves the cursor on `B29`, which also fails.

Concrete input: bug id `B30`, item title `fixes bugs B29, B31 and B30`. `named.search` matches (so the item is not skipped), but `claims_fix.search` returns `None`, so `_show_bug` classifies the item under `mentioned_by` instead of `fixing`. That is exactly the convention the inline comment promises to support ("the verb, then the id or a list holding it": `"fixes bugs A, B and X"`), and the docstring names the same form. Consequently `ddflow show B30` (and any consumer of the `fixing` list, e.g. the fix-task view) treats the true fix task as a mere mention. Only the first element of an and-joined list, or an element sitting immediately after a comma (`fixes bugs B29, B30`), is matched; `fixes bugs B29 and B30` fails for `B30` as well.

(The rest of the file is internally consistent: the exit-code contracts in `loops`/`recover`, the truncation direction and `_render`-after-`_bound` ordering in `status`, the `not removed` filtering in `_dependency_findings`, the fallback→note mapping in `_launcher_findings`, the `shards - {log.shard.name}` self-exclusion in `_unknown_author_notes`, and the `inspect.signature` arity check in `render` all match their comments and docstrings.)

chunk_findings.detail: The truncation knob moved out of the module that used to be `ddflow.api.reporting`. `_bound` reads `STATUS_LIST_LIMIT` as a global of the new area module `ddflow.api.reporting.overview`, and `status` calls the `_load` name bound in that same module's namespace. The package `__init__` re-exports these names, so `ddflow.api.reporting.STATUS_LIST_LIMIT` still resolves and `import ddflow.api.reporting` still "works" — but rebinding the package attribute is now a silent no-op with respect to behavior. Concretely: a test that exercises the bounded MCP body (the 721k-char case this constant exists for) via `monkeypatch.setattr("ddflow.api.reporting.STATUS_LIST_LIMIT", 2)` and then calls `status(repo)` will still get lists sliced at 25, because `_bound` looks up `STATUS_LIST_LIMIT` in `overview`'s globals, not the package re-export; the same applies to any caller patching `ddflow.api.reporting._load` to stub the repo load, since `status` invokes the `_load` bound in `overview`, not the re-exported one. The stated mechanical verification (AST identity + byte-identical goldens) cannot catch this, because it is only observable through an attribute rebind on the old path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/overview.py `STATUS_LIST_LIMIT` / `status` / `_bound`

chunk_findings.detail:
`worktree_entries` builds its untracked list with `_git_z(root, "ls-files", "--others", "--exclude-standard", "-z")`, i.e. with **no** `FINGERPRINT_EXCLUDE` / `_ours` filtering, and then applies the cost guard `if len(untracked) > MAX_UNTRACKED_HASHED: return None` *before* the `_ours(path)` filter inside the loop. The sibling helper in the same module, `_untracked_paths` (used by `_untracked_digest` and `diff_stat`), does the opposite: it passes `*FINGERPRINT_EXCLUDE` and therefore excludes `.ddflow/`. So the two halves of the same evidence disagree about what counts as "untracked".

Concretely: the whole reason `FINGERPRINT_EXCLUDE` exists (per its own comment) is that `.ddflow/` is *not* gitignored and was "creeping into a fingerprint"; `--exclude-standard` therefore does not drop it. Take a repository where `.ddflow/` has accumulated more than 512 untracked bookkeeping files (e.g. one event file per gate run) and no other untracked files. `_untracked_paths` returns `[]`, so `tree_fingerprint`/`_untracked_digest` behave normally; but `worktree_entries` sees `len(untracked) == 513 > 512` and returns `None`, so `source_tree(cwd)` silently returns `""` for every call even though none of those 513 files would ever be hashed (they are all dropped by `_ours`). Content-based evidence (`source_tree`/`commit_source_tree` comparisons, etc.) is thus disabled by ddflow's own state directory — exactly the class of "un-ignored directory full of artifacts" that `MAX_UNTRACKED_HASHED`'s comment says it wants to survive. Moving the guard after the `_ours` filter (or filtering the untracked list the same way `_untracked_paths` does) fixes it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/evidence.py:worktree_entries

chunk_findings.detail: `verify` and `verify_regression_test` read the gate runner through their own module globals: `from .runner import run_command_gate` (and `load_gates` on line 12) binds the name at import time. Before the split both names lived in `ddflow.services.gates`, so a caller/test that stubbed them via the package attribute (e.g. `monkeypatch.setattr("ddflow.services.gates.run_command_gate", fake)` or `monkeypatch.setattr(gates, "run_command_gate", fake)`) changed what `verify` called. After the move the package only re-exports the name; rebinding `ddflow.services.gates.run_command_gate` does not touch `mutation.run_command_gate`, so `verify` silently calls the real gate binary instead of the stub. Concretely, the probe referenced in the docstring (`tests/test_gate_verify.py`), which must control pass/fail per mutation to demonstrate the vacuous-pass guard, either now executes real commands (a test that intends to simulate `outcome == "failed"` instead gets the real outcome and can no longer assert `verified`) or fails outright; the same applies to any caller that stubs `load_gates` for `verify_regression_test`. This is a behaviour change the "AST-identical / byte-identical goldens" checks cannot see, and it is the exact package-attribute rebinding gap the move introduces.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/mutation.py:12-13

chunk_findings.detail: These two tests impose contradictory requirements on a package attribute whose name equals an area module's name, so the suite cannot pass for `ddflow.api.reporting` and `ddflow.api.knowledge`. `test_an_area_is_reachable_as_its_module` requires `getattr(pkg, "status") is <the status submodule>` (likewise for `doctor`, `render`, `progress`, and knowledge's `recall`). But `status`/`doctor`/`render`/`progress`/`recall` are in `DEFINED`, and since the `__init__` may define nothing, each must be bound as a top-level def/class/assign inside some area module; `_top_level_names` collects exactly those, so `test_every_name_an_area_binds_is_the_same_object_on_the_package` requires `getattr(pkg, "status") is <that bound object>`. A function/constant is never the module object, so one of the two assertions must fail (whichever wins the last binding in the `__init__`): binding the area module as `reporting.status` makes `test_every_name_an_area_binds...` fail for the area that defines `status`; binding the defined object makes `test_an_area_is_reachable_as_its_module` fail. This directly contradicts the docstring claim "No area shares its name with a function: `gates.evidence` is the module" — that holds only for gates, not for reporting's `status`/`doctor`/`render`/`progress` nor knowledge's `recall`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_module_splits.py:test_an_area_is_reachable_as_its_module / test_every_name_an_area_binds_is_the_same_object_on_the_package

chunk_findings.detail: The package re-exports names *by value*, so rebinding a re-exported name on the package no longer reaches the code that reads it, contradicting the change's stated "same imports, no behaviour change" guarantee. Before the split, `ddflow.api.knowledge` *was* the defining module: functions such as `bug_found`/`bug_file_tasks`/`research_add`/`memory_add` read module globals like `BUG_REPORT_COMMAND`, `_load`, `Config`, `LINK_RELATIONS`, `recall`, etc. directly off that module, so a caller or test doing `from ddflow.api import knowledge as K; K.BUG_REPORT_COMMAND = "custom"` (or `monkeypatch.setattr(knowledge, "Config", fake)`, `knowledge._load = fake`) changed what those functions actually used. After this move, `bug_found` is defined in `ddflow/api/knowledge/bugs.py` and reads `bugs.BUG_REPORT_COMMAND`; `research_add` reads `research.Config`/its own `_load`, etc. Rebinding `ddflow.api.knowledge.BUG_REPORT_COMMAND` (the only public location that existed pre-split, and the only one a pre-existing test could have used) is now silently ignored, so such a test or caller exercises the real constant/helper instead of the patched one — a genuine runtime behaviour change, not a pure move. The in-file docstring documents the new patch-the-defining-module rule, but that confirms the semantic change and does not restore the old patch point.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/__init__.py (package re-export block, `from .bugs`/`from .lessons`/`from ...config`/`from ...core.model`/`from .._base` bindings)

chunk_findings.detail: Before the split, `_store` was a top-level function of the single module `ddflow/api/knowledge.py`, so *every* caller in that module (including `memory_list`) resolved it through the module's own globals. Tests/plugins that injected a fake index did so by rebinding the module attribute, e.g. `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.api.knowledge, "_store", fake)`, and every list/search function in the file picked it up. After the move, `_store` lives in the sibling area `lessons.py`, and `memory.py` binds it into its own globals at import time (`from .lessons import _store`). `memory_list` now reads that binding, not the re-exported package attribute. Concretely: with such a patch in place, `memory_list(repo, query="x")` still executes the real `_store(repo, log, cfg)` (the `store = _store(...)` call in the `if query:` branch) instead of the injected double, so the patch silently no-ops — the query path returns whatever the real search store produces rather than the stubbed data the test asserts on. This is the one name in this file whose patch semantics actually change: `O`, `IDS`, `csv_list` and `_load` were already imported from other modules before the split, so rebinding `ddflow.api.knowledge.<name>` never reached these bodies; `_store` did, because it was defined in the hot module.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/memory.py: from .lessons import _store (used in memory_list)

chunk_findings.detail: `depth += {"[": 1, "]": -1}.get(ch, 0)` lets `depth` go negative when a parametrize value itself contains `]` — a case the sibling `_looks_like_several` explicitly declares supported (`t[x] y]` in its docstring, and it guards with `max(0, ...)`). Once `depth < 0`, every later `,`/`;` fails the `depth == 0` test and is never treated as a separator, so a comma-separated list is silently collapsed into one entry instead of being split. Concrete input: `--regression-test "tests/test_a.py::test_param[x]y],tests/missing.py::test_nope"`. `_split_outside_brackets` returns the whole string as one entry; `_unresolved_tests` then computes `path="tests/test_a.py"`, `names="test_param[x]y],tests/missing.py::test_nope"`, `wanted=["test_param"]`. `_looks_like_several` sees no whitespace outside brackets, so `tokens[1:]` is empty and it returns `False`; `_defines` finds `test_param` in `tests/test_a.py`, so the `not any(...)` arm is also `False`. The entry is therefore not added to `missing`, and `tests/missing.py::test_nope` is never resolved. `_unresolved_tests` returns `missing=[]` even though the second regression test does not exist, letting the bug be closed on a non-existent test. This is the same failure mode the `;` fix (B227585c781) was meant to eliminate — a list resolved as one node id. Clamping `depth` with `max(0, depth + {"[": 1, "]": -1}.get(ch, 0))`, as `_looks_like_several` already does, restores the split.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:_split_outside_brackets

chunk_findings.detail: The guard for CONFIRMED/REFUTED is `not (finding.probe or finding.probe_output)`, so a finding whose `probe` is empty but whose `probe_output` is non-empty is accepted. The function's own docstring says "a CONFIRMED with no probe is an opinion wearing a label", and the emitted error text says the verdict "requires a --probe (and ideally --probe-output)", i.e. `--probe` is mandatory and `--probe-output` is supplementary. Concrete input: `Finding(question="q", verdict="CONFIRMED", probe="", probe_output="ran pytest and saw X")` reaches line 57, passes the validation, and `research_add` returns `O.ok("research.recorded", ...)`; the intended rule would instead return the `O.failed` message demanding `--probe`. The OR lets the optional evidence field substitute for the required one.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/research.py:57

chunk_findings.detail: This package re-exports the moved names (`KEEP_RUN_LOGS`, `MAX_UNTRACKED_HASHED`, `EventLog`, `Config`, `run_command_gate`, …), but the moved functions read those names from their *own area module's* globals, so rebinding the package attribute no longer reaches any caller. Before the split there was one module, so a test or caller doing `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.services.gates, "KEEP_RUN_LOGS", False)` (or patching `gates.EventLog`, `gates.MAX_UNTRACKED_HASHED`, `gates.Config`, etc.) changed what `run_command_gate` observed. After the move, `run_command_gate` is defined in `ddflow.services.gates.runner` and resolves `KEEP_RUN_LOGS`/`EventLog` from that module's namespace; setting the same name on the package leaves the runner's binding untouched, so the gate still keeps run logs and still uses the real `EventLog` while the test believes it replaced them. The same silent no-op applies to every re-exported helper/constant, which directly contradicts the "no behaviour change" claim in the intent (the package docstring itself concedes "A REBINDING is not shared"). Any existing test/plugin that patches `ddflow.services.gates.<name>` will keep passing its old assertion only by accident or fail because the patched value is ignored.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/__init__.py:1

chunk_findings.detail: The call `W.git(cwd, "hash-object", *paths)` passes untracked paths with no `--` separator, unlike every other argv list in this same file (`_untracked_paths` and `diff_stat` pass `--`, and `_hash_into` passes `"--"` before the same kind of path list). Git's option parser permutes and accepts options after positional args, so an untracked file whose name begins with `-` is consumed as an option rather than a file. Concretely, in a repository containing an untracked file literally named `-w`, `paths` is `["-w", "real.txt"]`; git parses `-w` as "write the object" and hashes only `real.txt`, so (a) `hash-object` WRITES a loose object into `.git/objects`, violating this function's own stated invariant that the observer "writes nothing", and (b) `len(ids) != len(paths)` makes the function fall back to the weaker names-only digest for the whole tree, silently degrading `tree_fingerprint` (so `stale_evidence` goes quiet) in exactly the repositories that have such a file. A file named `--stdin` would additionally make git read stdin instead. Adding the `--` terminator before `*paths` fixes it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/evidence.py `_untracked_digest`

chunk_findings.detail: `family_of` imports `family_for` from `...config` inside the function body instead of at module level. If a caller or test patches the package’s re-exported name (`ddflow.services.gates.family_for`) to control the family mapping, the patch is silently ignored: `family_of` always reads `ddflow.config.family_for` directly. For example, after `monkeypatch.setattr(gates, "family_for", lambda model, families: "anthropic")`, calling `family_of("unknown-model", cfg)` still returns the real, unpatched lookup, so any test relying on dependency injection for family resolution tests the wrong thing.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/reviewers.py:family_of

chunk_findings.detail: `reviewer_independence` imports `router_set` from `...config` inside the function body. Patching the re-exported `ddflow.services.gates.router_set` has no effect on the router lookup. A test that sets `router_set` to return a router family list to exercise the router-author branch will instead call the real `router_set`, typically getting `None` and falling into a non-router code path, so the router-author logic is not actually exercised.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/reviewers.py:reviewer_independence

chunk_findings.detail: The move puts this code one package level deeper (the original module was `ddflow/services/gates.py`, i.e. package `ddflow.services`; the new file is `ddflow/services/gates/runner.py`, package `ddflow.services.gates`). Per the stated rule — "relative imports gain one dot because the code moved one package level down" — every *pre-existing* relative import must gain a dot, and the diff does exactly that for `..infra` → `...infra` (and for the in-function `...infra` imports of `tomlcfg`/`worktree`). The `testcmd` import, however, still has the original single dot. `testcmd` is not one of the gates domains this split creates (the plan lists `defs/run/evidence/outcomes`; `testcmd` is a dependency `gates.py` imported from, not part of `gates.py`), so it still lives at `ddflow/services/testcmd.py`. With `.testcmd` the interpreter resolves `ddflow.services.gates.testcmd`, which does not exist, so `import ddflow.services.gates.runner` raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ddflow.services.gates.testcmd'` at import time. Since `run_command_gate` is reached through the gates package re-export, every caller — `gate run`, the CLI/MCP `--help` and `tools/list` goldens the change claims are byte-identical — fails to import. The correct line is `from ..testcmd import suggested_test_command` (unless `testcmd.py` was also physically moved from `ddflow/services/` into `ddflow/services/gates/`, which the stated area list does not mention).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/runner.py:17 — `from .testcmd import suggested_test_command`

chunk_findings.detail: The exemption keys for the three moved knowledge writers were rewritten to `api/knowledge/bugs.py:_file_fix_task`, `api/knowledge/pairs.py:link_record` and `api/knowledge/bugs.py:bug_file_tasks`, but the knowledge package created by this change does not contain `bugs.py` or `pairs.py`. The change's own area list is `knowledge -> lessons/decisions/research/recall/memory`, and the sibling edit in the same diff confirms the file-name convention by moving `memory_add` to `api/knowledge/memory.py`. These functions therefore land in one of the five real areas (`link_record`, which "merges a lesson INTO the one it duplicates", is a `lessons`-domain writer; the `_file_fix_task`/`bug_file_tasks` pair is the `research`-domain bug-fix-task writer), so the defining path the coverage scanner sees (e.g. `api/knowledge/lessons.py:link_record`) never equals the dict key. Because `_calls_check_add`/`_appenders()` key writers by `<defining file path>:<function>` (as the surrounding assertions at lines 293-296 show), the `WRITERS_EXEMPT` lookup misses and the coherence assertion reports those writers as unexempted, failing the test. The fix is to key them by the area modules that actually exist (`lessons.py`/`research.py`, etc.), not the invented `bugs.py`/`pairs.py` paths.
chunk_findings.location: tests/test_coherence_coverage.py:149-151 (WRITERS_EXEMPT keys for the knowledge split)

chunk_findings.detail:
The test file is internally unsatisfiable for two of the three packages because the area-module names collide with names the same file insists the package must keep.

- `DEFINED["ddflow.api.reporting"]` contains `status`, `doctor`, `render`, `progress`; `DEFINED["ddflow.api.knowledge"]` contains `recall`.
- The stated split creates area modules named exactly `status`/`doctor`/`render`/`progress` (reporting) and `recall` (knowledge) — the intent lists those module names, and `test_an_area_is_reachable_as_its_module`'s own docstring uses `gates.evidence` from the same intent.

`test_an_area_is_reachable_as_its_module` asserts `getattr(pkg, "status") is <module ddflow.api.reporting.status>`. But once the `__init__` re-exports the original `status` name from whichever area defines it (`from .status import *` / `from .status import status`), the `IMPORT_FROM` bytecode stores the function into the package `__dict__` after importlib set the submodule attribute, so `pkg.status` is the function, not the module, and this test fails. Choose the other resolution — a bare `from . import status` so `pkg.status` stays the module — and `test_every_name_an_area_binds_is_the_same_object_on_the_package` fails instead: the area binds the function `status`, and it asserts `getattr(pkg, "status") is getattr(<area>, "status")`, i.e. module `is` function. There is no assignment of `pkg.status` that satisfies both, because a single attribute cannot be both the submodule and the re-exported callable. The same holds for `doctor`/`render`/`progress` and for `recall`; `gates` is unaffected only because `defs`/`run`/`evidence`/`outcomes` appear nowhere in its `DEFINED` list. Either the test as written cannot pass on the delivered tree, or the refactor silently rebinds `from ddflow.api.reporting import status` (and `recall`) from the function to a module — the exact break the change claims not to make.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_module_splits.py:118 (test_an_area_is_reachable_as_its_module / DEFINED)

chunk_findings.detail: The two confinement entries that replace the old `ddflow.services.gates -> subprocess` line (and the `-> tempfile` line) name `ddflow.services.gates.runner` / `ddflow.services.gates.evidence`, but the split described for this change is `gates -> defs/run/evidence/outcomes`. If the submodule is `gates/run.py`, then `ddflow.services.gates.runner` resolves to a module that does not exist: the real `gates/run.py` (which is the module the old single `gates.py`'s `subprocess`/`tempfile` usage moved into, given it is the one paired with `tempfile`) is no longer listed as a home for either dependency. The comment added to `ddflow/services/gates/__init__.py` ("`subprocess`, `tempfile` and `hashlib` ... each is confined to its one home by .importlinter") is therefore false for the `run` area — and because `import ddflow.services.gates` no longer pulls in `subprocess`/`tempfile`, nothing re-exports them either, so any contract/allowlist that rejects importers not named here will flag `gates/run.py`'s `subprocess`/`tempfile` imports. Either fix the entries to `ddflow.services.gates.run` (and keep the `evidence` ones) or correct the documented area name if the file really is `runner`.

chunk_findings.detail: The clamp fixes the reported direction (a trailing `]` after the id's closing `]` made depth negative and swallowed the following separator) but trades it for the opposite failure for any single node id whose param value contains two `]` and then a comma inside the id's brackets. `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]")` — the node id for `@pytest.mark.parametrize("s", ["a]b]c,d"])` — traces as: `[`→1, `]`→0, second `]`→`max(0,-1)=0`, then `,` is seen at depth 0 and splits, returning `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c", "d]"]`. Under the old code the second `]` drove depth to -1, so the `,` was kept and the function returned the single entry `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]"]` — which is the correct parse (the comma is inside the id's brackets). The clamped version therefore rejects a regression test that actually exists: `_unresolved_tests` will check `tests/a.py::test[a]b]c` and `d]`, find neither, and report the valid node id as missing. This is the mirror image of the bug being fixed, so the `max(0, ...)` heuristic is only sound when the deeper `]` is the id's final character; it needs the same treatment its sibling `_looks_like_several` gets or a bracket-count that is not reset by an in-value `]`.

chunk_findings.detail: The replacement list pattern `(?:[\w-]+(?:\s*,\s*(?:and\s+)?|\s+and\s+))*` is ambiguous, because the optional `and\s+` inside the comma-alternative and the following iteration's `[\w-]+` both match a bare `and`. A task title such as `"T (fixes A" + ", and"*60 + " )"` therefore has exponentially many parses (each `and` can be consumed either as the trailing `and` of one separator or as the next word). Since the bug id never appears anywhere, `re` must exhaust every one of those parses before concluding no match; because `_show_bug` runs `claims_fix` over every task title for every `ddflow show <bug>`, that single title hangs the command. The pre-change pattern `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*` had no overlap between the per-iteration word and separator and matched in linear time, so this cost is newly introduced by the diff. (The functional cases in the new test — `A and X`, `A, B and X`, `A, B, and X` — do match correctly; the defect is the backtracking blow-up on the non-matching sibling.)

chunk_findings.detail: The separator between an "element" and the following token is written as `*`, so an element is allowed to be a bare `[\w-]+` with no `,`/` and` after it. The outer `*` can then feed the next `[\w-]+` with the rest of the same token (regex backtracking happily splits a word), which means the id no longer has to start on a word boundary. Concretely, with bug id `B0` and a task titled `"Fixes AB0"`: `[\w-]+` matches `A`, the inner separator group matches zero times, and the literal `B0` then matches the `B0` suffix of `AB0` (the trailing `(?![\w-])` succeeds at end-of-string). `claims_fix` therefore reports the bug as `fixing`, even though `B0` is embedded in the unrelated token `AB0`. The sibling regex on the line above (`named`, with its `(?<![\w-])` lookbehind) deliberately refuses to match an id embedded in a word, so the two now disagree about the same text. The previous pattern could not over-match here: its element was `[\w-]+\s*,\s*`, i.e. the separator was mandatory, so the id could only be reached right after the verb's whitespace, `, ` or `and `. The regression test never exercises this shape (its `SEE` case has a space before the id, which still fails), so it does not catch it. Requiring one or more separators — `(?:\s*,\s*(?:and\s+)?|\s+and\s+)+` inside the element — restores the boundary while preserving all the intended list forms.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic decides a `]` closes the parametrize id's brackets whenever the next character is `""`, `,`, `;` or whitespace. But the whole reason for this bug is that a parametrize value may itself contain `]`, and such a value may also contain `,`/`;` (the sibling test `tests/a.py::t[1,2;3]` already asserts commas/semicolons inside brackets must not split). When the embedded `]` is immediately followed by a separator, the code wrongly treats it as the closing bracket.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b]")`. Tracing line 86-88: at `[`, `inside=True`; the `a` is appended; at the first `]`, `spec[i+1]` is `','`, so `after in ",;"` is true and `inside` is set to `False`; the following `,` then hits `if ch in ",;" and not inside` and splits. The call returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]']` (and the two-entry list `"tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/b.py::u"` returns three entries `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]', 'tests/b.py::u']`) instead of the single entry `tests/a.py::t[a],b]`. This is structurally identical to the case the new test covers (`tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]`, where the embedded `]` happens to be followed by `b` rather than the comma): one `[`, two `]`, comma between them; the outcome flips purely on the character after the first `]`, so `t[a],b]` is split inside its own brackets while `t[a]b]c,d]` is not. A value like `t[a] b,c]` (embedded `]` followed by whitespace then a comma) fails the same way via `after.isspace()`. The result is a spurious extra entry (e.g. `b]`) that `_unresolved_tests` will see as a missing test, i.e. the same "missing test never resolved / wrong resolution" failure mode this change was meant to eliminate.

chunk_findings.detail:
Given `spec = "tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"` (a real parametrize id `[a],b`, i.e. the inner list `[a]` plus a comma, wrapped by pytest's outer `[...]`):

- Trace of the new code: `[` → `inside=True`; `[` → `inside=True`; `]` with `after=","` → `inside = not True = False`; then `,` is seen while `not inside` → the string is split at the comma; the trailing `]` is ignored because `inside` is already `False`.
- Actual result: `["tests/a.py::t[[a]", "b]"]` — one node id became two fragments.
- Correct result (and what the *removed* clamped code produced): `["tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"]`. Under the old code `[[` drove `depth` to 2, the interior `]` decremented it to 1 (still > 0), so the comma inside the brackets did not split; the final `]` closed it correctly.

So this change regresses inputs that the clamped version handled. The comma here is inside the outer bracket, so `_unresolved_tests` will now receive the bogus fragment `tests/a.py::t[[a]` and fail to match the actual test — the same class of failure (a valid entry not resolved / a non-existent test reported) that Bfc9daca269 is about. The same happens for an interior `]` followed by whitespace, e.g. `"tests/a.py::t[[a] b,c]"` → `["tests/a.py::t[[a] b", "c]"]`.

The added test only exercises interior `]` followed by `]` (`t[[1]]`) or by a non-separator, so it never hits the `after in ",;" or after.isspace()` path on an interior bracket that still has a matching `]` later.

chunk_findings.detail: The change is supposed to fix Bfc863d295f, whose root cause is the `claims_fix` regex in `api/reporting/records._show_bug` requiring a comma after every list element (`(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*(?:and\s+)?ID`). No hunk in this diff modifies that regex or any other source file — the only functional change is a new test. Therefore the documented behavior is not implemented: README now states that "names X in a fix list ("fixes bugs A, B and X")" counts as a fix, but for a task titled `fixes bugs A1, A2 and Bfc863d295f` the `A2` element still requires a following comma, hits ` and` instead, and the whole match fails, so bug `Bfc863d295f` is still reported under `mentioned_by` rather than `fixing`. The README line asserts a behavior that the shipped code does not have.

chunk_findings.detail: The added test is the claimed regression test for Bfc863d295f, but it only asserts negative outcomes — it requires `body["fixing"] == []` and `body["mentioned_by"] == ["MANY", "WORD"]`, i.e. exactly the pre-fix behavior. It never asserts the positive cases named in the intent ("fixes bugs A1, A2 and X" / "fixes bugs A1 and X" ⇒ X is in `fixing`) that the unfixed code fails on. Both constructed titles already fail to match the unfixed pattern: `MANY` has a `)` before the id so no separator sequence terminates at the id, and in `WORD` the only id occurrences are `A<bid>` (prefixed), `<bid>x` (embedded in a word), and the trailing one reachable only after the non-comma token `see`. So the assertions hold on the unfixed code, the test passes before the fix, and registering it as `--regression-test` would close the bug without exercising the behavior it is meant to guard.

chunk_findings.detail: The separator between an "element" and the following token is written as `*`, so an element is allowed to be a bare `[\w-]+` with no `,`/` and` after it. The outer `*` can then feed the next `[\w-]+` with the rest of the same token (regex backtracking happily splits a word), which means the id no longer has to start on a word boundary. Concretely, with bug id `B0` and a task titled `"Fixes AB0"`: `[\w-]+` matches `A`, the inner separator group matches zero times, and the literal `B0` then matches the `B0` suffix of `AB0` (the trailing `(?![\w-])` succeeds at end-of-string). `claims_fix` therefore reports the bug as `fixing`, even though `B0` is embedded in the unrelated token `AB0`. The sibling regex on the line above (`named`, with its `(?<![\w-])` lookbehind) deliberately refuses to match an id embedded in a word, so the two now disagree about the same text. The previous pattern could not over-match here: its element was `[\w-]+\s*,\s*`, i.e. the separator was mandatory, so the id could only be reached right after the verb's whitespace, `, ` or `and `. The regression test never exercises this shape (its `SEE` case has a space before the id, which still fails), so it does not catch it. Requiring one or more separators — `(?:\s*,\s*(?:and\s+)?|\s+and\s+)+` inside the element — restores the boundary while preserving all the intended list forms.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/records.py (claims_fix regex, the `(?:[\w-]+(?:\s*,\s*(?:and\s+)?|\s+and\s+))*` fragment)

chunk_findings.detail: The change does not touch the claims-fix regex at all — the diff modifies only `README.md` and this test file, so `api/reporting/records._show_bug`'s pattern `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*(?:and\s+)?ID` is unchanged. The new test is therefore not a regression test for Bfc863d295f: every input it builds is a *negative* case ("this id is not a fix"), and all of them already produce no match under the pre-fix regex. In `MANY` the id sits after `" ) "`, so the list pattern can never reach it; in `WORD` the id is embedded (`A<bid>`, `<bid>x`) or preceded by the plain word `see` (`..., see <bid>`), neither of which is a comma or `and` separator in the list. So on the unfixed code both tasks land in `mentioned_by` and the assertions `fixing == [] and mentioned_by == ["MANY", "WORD"]` hold — the test passes before any fix, violating the required "watch it FAIL on the unfixed code". The bug's actual failing inputs (`fixes bugs A1, A2 and X`, `fixes bugs A1 and X` → X must be in `fixing`) appear nowhere in the added assertions, so if the regex is later changed or regressed the test still cannot detect it. Concretely: add a task titled e.g. `fixes bugs A1 and {bid}` and assert `bid` is in `fixing`; that is the case that currently fails and the one this change never exercises. (The README edit on lines 2263-2264 likewise now documents behavior — "or names X in a fix list ('fixes bugs A, B and X'), is a fix" — that this diff does not implement.)

chunk_findings.detail: The clamp fixes the reported direction (a trailing `]` after the id's closing `]` made depth negative and swallowed the following separator) but trades it for the opposite failure for any single node id whose param value contains two `]` and then a comma inside the id's brackets. `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]")` — the node id for `@pytest.mark.parametrize("s", ["a]b]c,d"])` — traces as: `[`→1, `]`→0, second `]`→`max(0,-1)=0`, then `,` is seen at depth 0 and splits, returning `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c", "d]"]`. Under the old code the second `]` drove depth to -1, so the `,` was kept and the function returned the single entry `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]"]` — which is the correct parse (the comma is inside the id's brackets). The clamped version therefore rejects a regression test that actually exists: `_unresolved_tests` will check `tests/a.py::test[a]b]c` and `d]`, find neither, and report the valid node id as missing. This is the mirror image of the bug being fixed, so the `max(0, ...)` heuristic is only sound when the deeper `]` is the id's final character; it needs the same treatment its sibling `_looks_like_several` gets or a bracket-count that is not reset by an in-value `]`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic decides a `]` closes the parametrize id's brackets whenever the next character is `""`, `,`, `;` or whitespace. But the whole reason for this bug is that a parametrize value may itself contain `]`, and such a value may also contain `,`/`;` (the sibling test `tests/a.py::t[1,2;3]` already asserts commas/semicolons inside brackets must not split). When the embedded `]` is immediately followed by a separator, the code wrongly treats it as the closing bracket.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b]")`. Tracing line 86-88: at `[`, `inside=True`; the `a` is appended; at the first `]`, `spec[i+1]` is `','`, so `after in ",;"` is true and `inside` is set to `False`; the following `,` then hits `if ch in ",;" and not inside` and splits. The call returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]']` (and the two-entry list `"tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/b.py::u"` returns three entries `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]', 'tests/b.py::u']`) instead of the single entry `tests/a.py::t[a],b]`. This is structurally identical to the case the new test covers (`tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]`, where the embedded `]` happens to be followed by `b` rather than the comma): one `[`, two `]`, comma between them; the outcome flips purely on the character after the first `]`, so `t[a],b]` is split inside its own brackets while `t[a]b]c,d]` is not. A value like `t[a] b,c]` (embedded `]` followed by whitespace then a comma) fails the same way via `after.isspace()`. The result is a spurious extra entry (e.g. `b]`) that `_unresolved_tests` will see as a missing test, i.e. the same "missing test never resolved / wrong resolution" failure mode this change was meant to eliminate.

chunk_findings.detail: Over-split: any bracketed parametrize value containing a comma followed by a token ending in `.py` is torn apart, even though the comma is inside the id's brackets. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]")`: after `[` `bracketed=True`, every `,`/`;` is tested against `_NEXT_PATH.match(spec, i+1)`; at the comma the remainder is `b.py]`, which the regex matches (`[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` matches `.py`, `(?![\w.])` sees `]`), so it splits. The function returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b.py]']` instead of the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]']`. This is exactly the case the new test `test_a_value_whose_inner_bracket_meets_a_separator_stays_one_entry` covers for `t[a],b]` — it only passes because `b]` lacks the `.py`; the sibling input `t[a.py,b.py]` fails the same way (returns `['tests/a.py::t[a.py', 'b.py]']`). The pre-change code (comma suppressed while `inside`) returned one entry here, so this is a regression introduced by the diff, and the new tests do not exercise a value token ending in `.py`.

chunk_findings.detail: Under-split: once an entry is bracketed, a following separator is ignored unless the next entry starts with a file path, so a legitimate non-path entry is merged. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x")`: at the comma `bracketed=True` and the remainder ` pytest -k x` contains no `.py`, so no split; the result is the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x']`. The function's own contract ("entries separated by ',' or ';'") and the newly added `test_entries_without_brackets_split_as_before` treat `pytest -k x` as a separate entry (it splits there only because no `[` preceded it), so the behavior is inconsistent and the command is swallowed into the node id, which is the same failure mode (an entry that is never seen as its own item) that this change set out to fix.

chunk_findings.detail: The replacement list pattern `(?:[\w-]+(?:\s*,\s*(?:and\s+)?|\s+and\s+))*` is ambiguous, because the optional `and\s+` inside the comma-alternative and the following iteration's `[\w-]+` both match a bare `and`. A task title such as `"T (fixes A" + ", and"*60 + " )"` therefore has exponentially many parses (each `and` can be consumed either as the trailing `and` of one separator or as the next word). Since the bug id never appears anywhere, `re` must exhaust every one of those parses before concluding no match; because `_show_bug` runs `claims_fix` over every task title for every `ddflow show <bug>`, that single title hangs the command. The pre-change pattern `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*` had no overlap between the per-iteration word and separator and matched in linear time, so this cost is newly introduced by the diff. (The functional cases in the new test — `A and X`, `A, B and X`, `A, B, and X` — do match correctly; the defect is the backtracking blow-up on the non-matching sibling.)

chunk_findings.detail:
Given `spec = "tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"` (a real parametrize id `[a],b`, i.e. the inner list `[a]` plus a comma, wrapped by pytest's outer `[...]`):

- Trace of the new code: `[` → `inside=True`; `[` → `inside=True`; `]` with `after=","` → `inside = not True = False`; then `,` is seen while `not inside` → the string is split at the comma; the trailing `]` is ignored because `inside` is already `False`.
- Actual result: `["tests/a.py::t[[a]", "b]"]` — one node id became two fragments.
- Correct result (and what the *removed* clamped code produced): `["tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"]`. Under the old code `[[` drove `depth` to 2, the interior `]` decremented it to 1 (still > 0), so the comma inside the brackets did not split; the final `]` closed it correctly.

So this change regresses inputs that the clamped version handled. The comma here is inside the outer bracket, so `_unresolved_tests` will now receive the bogus fragment `tests/a.py::t[[a]` and fail to match the actual test — the same class of failure (a valid entry not resolved / a non-existent test reported) that Bfc9daca269 is about. The same happens for an interior `]` followed by whitespace, e.g. `"tests/a.py::t[[a] b,c]"` → `["tests/a.py::t[[a] b", "c]"]`.

The added test only exercises interior `]` followed by `]` (`t[[1]]`) or by a non-separator, so it never hits the `after in ",;" or after.isspace()` path on an interior bracket that still has a matching `]` later.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic only splits a bracketed entry when the text following the separator never makes the bracket depth negative, and `_closes_unopened` scans the *entire remaining string* — including later entries. A later entry whose parametrize id itself contains an unmatched `]` therefore cancels an otherwise legitimate split, merging the whole list into one entry. This is exactly the shape the module documents/test as valid (`t[a],b]`, `t[x]y]`) and it reproduces bug Bfc9daca269.

Concretely, `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d],e]")`:

- at the comma after `t[a]`, `cur` ends in `]`, but `_closes_unopened("b],tests/c.py::d],e]")` hits the `]` after `b` and returns True → no split;
- at the comma after `t[a],b]`, `cur` ends in `]`, but `_closes_unopened("tests/c.py::d],e]")` hits the `]` after `d` and returns True → no split again.

Result: `["tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d],e]"]` (one entry), whereas the correct answer is `["tests/a.py::t[a],b]", "tests/c.py::d],e]"]`. The pre-change code split here, because `_NEXT_PATH` matched `tests/c.py` after the second comma, so this is a behavioral regression introduced by the change, not a pre-existing limitation. Note the added test `("tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d[e]", ...)` deliberately uses a *balanced* second id (`d[e]`), which is why it passes; the `d],e]` variant (a value holding `]` and `,`, explicitly listed as supported in the docstring) fails. The same root cause also blocks a split when a command following a bracketed id contains a `]` (e.g. `tests/a.py::t[x], pytest -k "a]b"`).

Because the missing second node id is never separated, `_unresolved_tests` again evaluates it as part of the first token, so a nonexistent regression test can be accepted — the very failure Bfc9daca269 intends to fix.

chunk_findings.detail: The clamp fixes the reported direction (a trailing `]` after the id's closing `]` made depth negative and swallowed the following separator) but trades it for the opposite failure for any single node id whose param value contains two `]` and then a comma inside the id's brackets. `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]")` — the node id for `@pytest.mark.parametrize("s", ["a]b]c,d"])` — traces as: `[`→1, `]`→0, second `]`→`max(0,-1)=0`, then `,` is seen at depth 0 and splits, returning `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c", "d]"]`. Under the old code the second `]` drove depth to -1, so the `,` was kept and the function returned the single entry `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]"]` — which is the correct parse (the comma is inside the id's brackets). The clamped version therefore rejects a regression test that actually exists: `_unresolved_tests` will check `tests/a.py::test[a]b]c` and `d]`, find neither, and report the valid node id as missing. This is the mirror image of the bug being fixed, so the `max(0, ...)` heuristic is only sound when the deeper `]` is the id's final character; it needs the same treatment its sibling `_looks_like_several` gets or a bracket-count that is not reset by an in-value `]`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic decides a `]` closes the parametrize id's brackets whenever the next character is `""`, `,`, `;` or whitespace. But the whole reason for this bug is that a parametrize value may itself contain `]`, and such a value may also contain `,`/`;` (the sibling test `tests/a.py::t[1,2;3]` already asserts commas/semicolons inside brackets must not split). When the embedded `]` is immediately followed by a separator, the code wrongly treats it as the closing bracket.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b]")`. Tracing line 86-88: at `[`, `inside=True`; the `a` is appended; at the first `]`, `spec[i+1]` is `','`, so `after in ",;"` is true and `inside` is set to `False`; the following `,` then hits `if ch in ",;" and not inside` and splits. The call returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]']` (and the two-entry list `"tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/b.py::u"` returns three entries `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]', 'tests/b.py::u']`) instead of the single entry `tests/a.py::t[a],b]`. This is structurally identical to the case the new test covers (`tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]`, where the embedded `]` happens to be followed by `b` rather than the comma): one `[`, two `]`, comma between them; the outcome flips purely on the character after the first `]`, so `t[a],b]` is split inside its own brackets while `t[a]b]c,d]` is not. A value like `t[a] b,c]` (embedded `]` followed by whitespace then a comma) fails the same way via `after.isspace()`. The result is a spurious extra entry (e.g. `b]`) that `_unresolved_tests` will see as a missing test, i.e. the same "missing test never resolved / wrong resolution" failure mode this change was meant to eliminate.

chunk_findings.detail: Over-split: any bracketed parametrize value containing a comma followed by a token ending in `.py` is torn apart, even though the comma is inside the id's brackets. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]")`: after `[` `bracketed=True`, every `,`/`;` is tested against `_NEXT_PATH.match(spec, i+1)`; at the comma the remainder is `b.py]`, which the regex matches (`[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` matches `.py`, `(?![\w.])` sees `]`), so it splits. The function returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b.py]']` instead of the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]']`. This is exactly the case the new test `test_a_value_whose_inner_bracket_meets_a_separator_stays_one_entry` covers for `t[a],b]` — it only passes because `b]` lacks the `.py`; the sibling input `t[a.py,b.py]` fails the same way (returns `['tests/a.py::t[a.py', 'b.py]']`). The pre-change code (comma suppressed while `inside`) returned one entry here, so this is a regression introduced by the diff, and the new tests do not exercise a value token ending in `.py`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:_split_outside_brackets (`_NEXT_PATH` + `bracketed` condition)

chunk_findings.detail: Under-split: once an entry is bracketed, a following separator is ignored unless the next entry starts with a file path, so a legitimate non-path entry is merged. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x")`: at the comma `bracketed=True` and the remainder ` pytest -k x` contains no `.py`, so no split; the result is the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x']`. The function's own contract ("entries separated by ',' or ';'") and the newly added `test_entries_without_brackets_split_as_before` treat `pytest -k x` as a separate entry (it splits there only because no `[` preceded it), so the behavior is inconsistent and the command is swallowed into the node id, which is the same failure mode (an entry that is never seen as its own item) that this change set out to fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:_split_outside_brackets (`_NEXT_PATH` + `bracketed` condition)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_closes_unopened` scans the *entire* remainder `spec[i+1:]`, which includes the following entries, so an unbalanced `]` inside the *second* entry's parametrize value is misread as "closing a bracket the current entry never opened", and the split is suppressed.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]")`.

- At the comma, `cur == "tests/a.py::t[x]"` ends with `]` (first condition passes).
- `rest == "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"`. Walking it: `[` → depth 1, the first `]` → depth 0, then the trailing `]` → depth −1, so `_closes_unopened` returns `True`.
- The `and not _closes_unopened(...)` term is therefore `False`, the separator is appended to `cur`, and the function returns the single entry `["tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]` instead of the two entries `["tests/a.py::t[x]", "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]`.

The docstring itself declares `t[x]y]` a legitimate parametrize id, so `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is a valid second entry (its value is `a]b`). Because the list is not split, `_unresolved_tests` only looks at `tests/a.py::t` and the genuinely missing `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is never flagged — precisely the failure mode Bfc9daca269 is supposed to close, still reachable whenever the second bracketed entry's value contains a `]`. The added test only covers a second entry with balanced brackets (`tests/c.py::d[e]`), so it does not exercise this case.

Note this is a regression relative to the removed `_NEXT_PATH` approach, which matched the second entry by its leading `… .py` token and split correctly here.

chunk_findings.detail: The replacement list pattern `(?:[\w-]+(?:\s*,\s*(?:and\s+)?|\s+and\s+))*` is ambiguous, because the optional `and\s+` inside the comma-alternative and the following iteration's `[\w-]+` both match a bare `and`. A task title such as `"T (fixes A" + ", and"*60 + " )"` therefore has exponentially many parses (each `and` can be consumed either as the trailing `and` of one separator or as the next word). Since the bug id never appears anywhere, `re` must exhaust every one of those parses before concluding no match; because `_show_bug` runs `claims_fix` over every task title for every `ddflow show <bug>`, that single title hangs the command. The pre-change pattern `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*` had no overlap between the per-iteration word and separator and matched in linear time, so this cost is newly introduced by the diff. (The functional cases in the new test — `A and X`, `A, B and X`, `A, B, and X` — do match correctly; the defect is the backtracking blow-up on the non-matching sibling.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/records.py:claims_fix

chunk_findings.detail: The change is supposed to fix Bfc863d295f, whose root cause is the `claims_fix` regex in `api/reporting/records._show_bug` requiring a comma after every list element (`(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*(?:and\s+)?ID`). No hunk in this diff modifies that regex or any other source file — the only functional change is a new test. Therefore the documented behavior is not implemented: README now states that "names X in a fix list ("fixes bugs A, B and X")" counts as a fix, but for a task titled `fixes bugs A1, A2 and Bfc863d295f` the `A2` element still requires a following comma, hits ` and` instead, and the whole match fails, so bug `Bfc863d295f` is still reported under `mentioned_by` rather than `fixing`. The README line asserts a behavior that the shipped code does not have.
chunk_findings.title: README.md:2262 (no hunk in api/reporting/records.py)

chunk_findings.detail: The added test is the claimed regression test for Bfc863d295f, but it only asserts negative outcomes — it requires `body["fixing"] == []` and `body["mentioned_by"] == ["MANY", "WORD"]`, i.e. exactly the pre-fix behavior. It never asserts the positive cases named in the intent ("fixes bugs A1, A2 and X" / "fixes bugs A1 and X" ⇒ X is in `fixing`) that the unfixed code fails on. Both constructed titles already fail to match the unfixed pattern: `MANY` has a `)` before the id so no separator sequence terminates at the id, and in `WORD` the only id occurrences are `A<bid>` (prefixed), `<bid>x` (embedded in a word), and the trailing one reachable only after the non-comma token `see`. So the assertions hold on the unfixed code, the test passes before the fix, and registering it as `--regression-test` would close the bug without exercising the behavior it is meant to guard.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_show_bug.py:128-146

chunk_findings.detail: The change's stated purpose is to fix bug Bfc863d295f, whose defect is localised in `api/reporting/records._show_bug`: its `claims_fix` regex `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*(?:and\s+)?ID` requires a comma after every preceding list element, so the convention named in its own comment is not matched. Concretely, for a title like `fixes bugs A1 and X` (and `fixes bugs A1, A2 and X`) the id `X` still does not match, and the fix task is still filed under `mentioned_by` instead of `fixing`. The diff does not touch that file at all — it only rewrites `ddflow/services/export/kind_worklog.py` to reuse `kind_changelog._fixed_bugs` (which addresses a different bug, `Bf228d082de`, per the comment and the new test's docstring) and adds `tests/test_export_worklog_fix_list.py`. That new test exercises solely the worklog line-folding path, so it can pass in full while the bug the change claims to fix (`records._show_bug` mis-classifying `fixes bugs A1 and X`) is completely unaddressed. The regression test required by the task description must call `records._show_bug` with an "and"-joined list and observe X classified as fixing; no such assertion exists here.
chunk_findings.title: api/reporting/records._show_bug (unchanged by this diff)

chunk_findings.detail: The new separator `r",|\s+and\s+"` requires whitespace on *both* sides of `and`, but the grammar this parser is supposed to mirror names `and` with only a trailing space requirement: `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*(?:and\s+)?ID`. That regex accepts an `and` that follows a comma with no space, so `_FIXES` captures a list like `A,B,and X` as `A,B,and X`, but the splitter then cannot break `and X` off, because there is no `\s+` before `and`. Concretely, `_fixed_bugs("fixes bugs A,B,and X")` now returns `["A", "B", "and X"]` (a bogus id `and X` plus a lost `X`), whereas the previous pattern `\band\b` returned `["A", "B", "X"]`. So this change trades the hyphenated-id bug for a regression on the comma-without-space form of the very same "and"-joined list (e.g. terse commit subjects `fixes bugs A,B,and X`), and the failure is exactly the class of bug being fixed: `X` is again attributed to `mentioned_by` rather than fixing. The added test only covers the spaced variants (`A, B, and X`, `A and X`), so it does not catch this; a separator that tolerates a missing leading space (e.g. `r",|\band\b(?![\w-])"` with a guard for `-and-`, or splitting on `\s*,\s*|\s+and\s+` while first protecting hyphenated ids) would cover both cases.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_changelog.py:192 (`_fixed_bugs`)

chunk_findings.detail: The separator between an "element" and the following token is written as `*`, so an element is allowed to be a bare `[\w-]+` with no `,`/` and` after it. The outer `*` can then feed the next `[\w-]+` with the rest of the same token (regex backtracking happily splits a word), which means the id no longer has to start on a word boundary. Concretely, with bug id `B0` and a task titled `"Fixes AB0"`: `[\w-]+` matches `A`, the inner separator group matches zero times, and the literal `B0` then matches the `B0` suffix of `AB0` (the trailing `(?![\w-])` succeeds at end-of-string). `claims_fix` therefore reports the bug as `fixing`, even though `B0` is embedded in the unrelated token `AB0`. The sibling regex on the line above (`named`, with its `(?<![\w-])` lookbehind) deliberately refuses to match an id embedded in a word, so the two now disagree about the same text. The previous pattern could not over-match here: its element was `[\w-]+\s*,\s*`, i.e. the separator was mandatory, so the id could only be reached right after the verb's whitespace, `, ` or `and `. The regression test never exercises this shape (its `SEE` case has a space before the id, which still fails), so it does not catch it. Requiring one or more separators — `(?:\s*,\s*(?:and\s+)?|\s+and\s+)+` inside the element — restores the boundary while preserving all the intended list forms.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/records.py (claims_fix regex, the `(?:[\w-]+(?:\s*,\s*(?:and\s+)?|\s+and\s+))*` fragment)

chunk_findings.detail: The change does not touch the claims-fix regex at all — the diff modifies only `README.md` and this test file, so `api/reporting/records._show_bug`'s pattern `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*(?:and\s+)?ID` is unchanged. The new test is therefore not a regression test for Bfc863d295f: every input it builds is a *negative* case ("this id is not a fix"), and all of them already produce no match under the pre-fix regex. In `MANY` the id sits after `" ) "`, so the list pattern can never reach it; in `WORD` the id is embedded (`A<bid>`, `<bid>x`) or preceded by the plain word `see` (`..., see <bid>`), neither of which is a comma or `and` separator in the list. So on the unfixed code both tasks land in `mentioned_by` and the assertions `fixing == [] and mentioned_by == ["MANY", "WORD"]` hold — the test passes before any fix, violating the required "watch it FAIL on the unfixed code". The bug's actual failing inputs (`fixes bugs A1, A2 and X`, `fixes bugs A1 and X` → X must be in `fixing`) appear nowhere in the added assertions, so if the regex is later changed or regressed the test still cannot detect it. Concretely: add a task titled e.g. `fixes bugs A1 and {bid}` and assert `bid` is in `fixing`; that is the case that currently fails and the one this change never exercises. (The README edit on lines 2263-2264 likewise now documents behavior — "or names X in a fix list ('fixes bugs A, B and X'), is a fix" — that this diff does not implement.)
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_show_bug.py:128 (`test_the_fix_list_pattern_neither_backtracks_nor_matches_inside_a_word`)

chunk_findings.detail: The stated purpose of this change is bug Bfc863d295f, whose defect is in `api/reporting/records._show_bug`'s `claims_fix` regex: `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*(?:and\s+)?ID` requires a comma after every list element, so the last id of an "and"-joined fix list never matches. The diff provided here does not touch `api/reporting/records.py` at all — it only rewrites the fix-list parsing in `kind_worklog.py` (and references a different bug id, `Bf228d082de`). Concretely, given a record whose text is `fixes bugs A1 and X` or `fixes bugs A1, A2 and X`, `_show_bug` still runs the unchanged comma-requiring regex, returns no match for `X`, and the fix task is still reported under `mentioned_by` rather than as fixing `X`. The new regression test only exercises the worklog export path (`registry.render_body("worklog", ...)`) and therefore cannot fail on the unfixed `_show_bug` behavior — it would pass or fail entirely independently of the bug the change claims to close. As submitted, the change does not fix the reported bug and its test does not cover the reported probe.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_worklog.py (whole change)

chunk_findings.detail: Changing the split pattern from `r",|\band\b"` to `r",|\s+and\s+"` makes the "and" separator require whitespace on *both* sides. That is fine for the canonical `A, B and X`, but it regresses any list where a comma is followed directly by `and` (or where `and` is adjacent to a comma/start with no leading space). Example: `_fixed_bugs("x (fixes bugs A,B,and X)")` now returns `["A", "B", "and X"]`, whereas the old regex returned `["A", "B", "X"]`. The real id `X` is silently dropped and a bogus id `and X` is emitted/exported; the same happens for `"A,and B"` (piece after the comma is `and B`, which has no leading whitespace to match `\s+and\s+`) and for `"A, B,and X"`. So for these inputs the parser reintroduces exactly the symptom the task set out to fix (X not recognized as fixed).

chunk_findings.detail: Over-split: any bracketed parametrize value containing a comma followed by a token ending in `.py` is torn apart, even though the comma is inside the id's brackets. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]")`: after `[` `bracketed=True`, every `,`/`;` is tested against `_NEXT_PATH.match(spec, i+1)`; at the comma the remainder is `b.py]`, which the regex matches (`[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` matches `.py`, `(?![\w.])` sees `]`), so it splits. The function returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b.py]']` instead of the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]']`. This is exactly the case the new test `test_a_value_whose_inner_bracket_meets_a_separator_stays_one_entry` covers for `t[a],b]` — it only passes because `b]` lacks the `.py`; the sibling input `t[a.py,b.py]` fails the same way (returns `['tests/a.py::t[a.py', 'b.py]']`). The pre-change code (comma suppressed while `inside`) returned one entry here, so this is a regression introduced by the diff, and the new tests do not exercise a value token ending in `.py`.

chunk_findings.detail: Under-split: once an entry is bracketed, a following separator is ignored unless the next entry starts with a file path, so a legitimate non-path entry is merged. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x")`: at the comma `bracketed=True` and the remainder ` pytest -k x` contains no `.py`, so no split; the result is the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x']`. The function's own contract ("entries separated by ',' or ';'") and the newly added `test_entries_without_brackets_split_as_before` treat `pytest -k x` as a separate entry (it splits there only because no `[` preceded it), so the behavior is inconsistent and the command is swallowed into the node id, which is the same failure mode (an entry that is never seen as its own item) that this change set out to fix.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_closes_unopened` scans the *entire* remainder `spec[i+1:]`, which includes the following entries, so an unbalanced `]` inside the *second* entry's parametrize value is misread as "closing a bracket the current entry never opened", and the split is suppressed.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]")`.

- At the comma, `cur == "tests/a.py::t[x]"` ends with `]` (first condition passes).
- `rest == "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"`. Walking it: `[` → depth 1, the first `]` → depth 0, then the trailing `]` → depth −1, so `_closes_unopened` returns `True`.
- The `and not _closes_unopened(...)` term is therefore `False`, the separator is appended to `cur`, and the function returns the single entry `["tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]` instead of the two entries `["tests/a.py::t[x]", "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]`.

The docstring itself declares `t[x]y]` a legitimate parametrize id, so `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is a valid second entry (its value is `a]b`). Because the list is not split, `_unresolved_tests` only looks at `tests/a.py::t` and the genuinely missing `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is never flagged — precisely the failure mode Bfc9daca269 is supposed to close, still reachable whenever the second bracketed entry's value contains a `]`. The added test only covers a second entry with balanced brackets (`tests/c.py::d[e]`), so it does not exercise this case.

Note this is a regression relative to the removed `_NEXT_PATH` approach, which matched the second entry by its leading `… .py` token and split correctly here.

chunk_findings.detail:
Input: `tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]`.

This is a single node id whose value is `a],b.py,c` (the documented shape `t[a],b]` generalised, i.e. the separator before `]` is inside the id, and the rest `b.py,c]` closes a `]` it never opened). On the *old* code the first comma sees `cur == "tests/x.py::t[a]"` (ends with `]`), and `_closes_unopened("b.py,c]")` is `True`, so the branch is not taken and the spec is correctly kept as one entry.

On the *new* code `_NEXT_PATH.match("b.py,c]", 0)` succeeds: `[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` consumes `.py`, and the lookahead `(?=::|[\s,;]|$)` matches the following `,`. So the entry is split at the first comma, `bracketed` is reset to `False`, and the remaining comma (now "outside brackets") splits again. The function returns three entries:

    ["tests/x.py::t[a]", "b.py", "c]"]   # after
    ["tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]"]         # before (correct)

`b.py` here is a fragment of the parametrize value, not a following test path, so `_unresolved_tests` now resolves bogus entries (`b.py`, `c]`) instead of the real one. The asymmetry is visible in the regex's own comment: `t[a],b.py]` is handled (the `]` is not in the lookahead set), but `t[a],b.py,c]` / `t[a],b.py::c]` are not — the new "a test path follows" reason overrides `_closes_unopened` even when the following `.py` token is a value rather than an entry.

chunk_findings.detail:
Given `spec = "tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"` (a real parametrize id `[a],b`, i.e. the inner list `[a]` plus a comma, wrapped by pytest's outer `[...]`):

- Trace of the new code: `[` → `inside=True`; `[` → `inside=True`; `]` with `after=","` → `inside = not True = False`; then `,` is seen while `not inside` → the string is split at the comma; the trailing `]` is ignored because `inside` is already `False`.
- Actual result: `["tests/a.py::t[[a]", "b]"]` — one node id became two fragments.
- Correct result (and what the *removed* clamped code produced): `["tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"]`. Under the old code `[[` drove `depth` to 2, the interior `]` decremented it to 1 (still > 0), so the comma inside the brackets did not split; the final `]` closed it correctly.

So this change regresses inputs that the clamped version handled. The comma here is inside the outer bracket, so `_unresolved_tests` will now receive the bogus fragment `tests/a.py::t[[a]` and fail to match the actual test — the same class of failure (a valid entry not resolved / a non-existent test reported) that Bfc9daca269 is about. The same happens for an interior `]` followed by whitespace, e.g. `"tests/a.py::t[[a] b,c]"` → `["tests/a.py::t[[a] b", "c]"]`.

The added test only exercises interior `]` followed by `]` (`t[[1]]`) or by a non-separator, so it never hits the `after in ",;" or after.isspace()` path on an interior bracket that still has a matching `]` later.
chunk_findings.title: `_split_outside_brackets` (ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py, the `elif ch == "]" and inside:` branch, ~line 80–86)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic only splits a bracketed entry when the text following the separator never makes the bracket depth negative, and `_closes_unopened` scans the *entire remaining string* — including later entries. A later entry whose parametrize id itself contains an unmatched `]` therefore cancels an otherwise legitimate split, merging the whole list into one entry. This is exactly the shape the module documents/test as valid (`t[a],b]`, `t[x]y]`) and it reproduces bug Bfc9daca269.

Concretely, `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d],e]")`:

- at the comma after `t[a]`, `cur` ends in `]`, but `_closes_unopened("b],tests/c.py::d],e]")` hits the `]` after `b` and returns True → no split;
- at the comma after `t[a],b]`, `cur` ends in `]`, but `_closes_unopened("tests/c.py::d],e]")` hits the `]` after `d` and returns True → no split again.

Result: `["tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d],e]"]` (one entry), whereas the correct answer is `["tests/a.py::t[a],b]", "tests/c.py::d],e]"]`. The pre-change code split here, because `_NEXT_PATH` matched `tests/c.py` after the second comma, so this is a behavioral regression introduced by the change, not a pre-existing limitation. Note the added test `("tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d[e]", ...)` deliberately uses a *balanced* second id (`d[e]`), which is why it passes; the `d],e]` variant (a value holding `]` and `,`, explicitly listed as supported in the docstring) fails. The same root cause also blocks a split when a command following a bracketed id contains a `]` (e.g. `tests/a.py::t[x], pytest -k "a]b"`).

Because the missing second node id is never separated, `_unresolved_tests` again evaluates it as part of the first token, so a nonexistent regression test can be accepted — the very failure Bfc9daca269 intends to fix.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `_NEXT_PATH` disjunct is OR-ed ahead of the `_closes_unopened` guard, so a `.py`-looking token after a `]` forces a split even when the rest closes a bracket the entry never opened (i.e. even when the comma is provably inside a parametrize id, the case `_closes_unopened` exists to protect). Input:

    _split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b.py,c]")

At the first comma `cur` is `tests/a.py::t[a]` (ends with `]`) and the rest is `b.py,c]`; `_NEXT_PATH` matches `b.py` because `.py` is followed by `,` (in the `[\s,;]` lookahead). So it splits, `bracketed` resets to `False`, and the second comma splits again via the `not bracketed` branch, yielding three entries `["tests/a.py::t[a]", "b.py", "c]"]`. The docstring this diff touches explicitly promises that a parametrize value may hold `]` and `,` (`t[a],b]` is one value); the old condition kept this as the single entry `tests/a.py::t[a],b.py,c]` because `_closes_unopened("b.py,c]")` is true and blocks the split. So a single bracketed id whose value contains a `.py` token followed by a separator is now shredded into spurious "test" entries, which then feed `_unresolved_tests` — exactly the failure class (wrong number of parsed tests) the change is meant to eliminate. The added regression cases all place the `.py` path after a separator that is *between* entries, so they do not cover this shape; e.g. `tests/a.py::t[a],b.py::c]` (rest `b.py::c]`) also matches `_NEXT_PATH` and splits a single id.

chunk_findings.detail: The separator between an "element" and the following token is written as `*`, so an element is allowed to be a bare `[\w-]+` with no `,`/` and` after it. The outer `*` can then feed the next `[\w-]+` with the rest of the same token (regex backtracking happily splits a word), which means the id no longer has to start on a word boundary. Concretely, with bug id `B0` and a task titled `"Fixes AB0"`: `[\w-]+` matches `A`, the inner separator group matches zero times, and the literal `B0` then matches the `B0` suffix of `AB0` (the trailing `(?![\w-])` succeeds at end-of-string). `claims_fix` therefore reports the bug as `fixing`, even though `B0` is embedded in the unrelated token `AB0`. The sibling regex on the line above (`named`, with its `(?<![\w-])` lookbehind) deliberately refuses to match an id embedded in a word, so the two now disagree about the same text. The previous pattern could not over-match here: its element was `[\w-]+\s*,\s*`, i.e. the separator was mandatory, so the id could only be reached right after the verb's whitespace, `, ` or `and `. The regression test never exercises this shape (its `SEE` case has a space before the id, which still fails), so it does not catch it. Requiring one or more separators — `(?:\s*,\s*(?:and\s+)?|\s+and\s+)+` inside the element — restores the boundary while preserving all the intended list forms.

chunk_findings.detail: The change does not touch the claims-fix regex at all — the diff modifies only `README.md` and this test file, so `api/reporting/records._show_bug`'s pattern `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*(?:and\s+)?ID` is unchanged. The new test is therefore not a regression test for Bfc863d295f: every input it builds is a *negative* case ("this id is not a fix"), and all of them already produce no match under the pre-fix regex. In `MANY` the id sits after `" ) "`, so the list pattern can never reach it; in `WORD` the id is embedded (`A<bid>`, `<bid>x`) or preceded by the plain word `see` (`..., see <bid>`), neither of which is a comma or `and` separator in the list. So on the unfixed code both tasks land in `mentioned_by` and the assertions `fixing == [] and mentioned_by == ["MANY", "WORD"]` hold — the test passes before any fix, violating the required "watch it FAIL on the unfixed code". The bug's actual failing inputs (`fixes bugs A1, A2 and X`, `fixes bugs A1 and X` → X must be in `fixing`) appear nowhere in the added assertions, so if the regex is later changed or regressed the test still cannot detect it. Concretely: add a task titled e.g. `fixes bugs A1 and {bid}` and assert `bid` is in `fixing`; that is the case that currently fails and the one this change never exercises. (The README edit on lines 2263-2264 likewise now documents behavior — "or names X in a fix list ('fixes bugs A, B and X'), is a fix" — that this diff does not implement.)

chunk_findings.detail: The stated purpose of this change is bug Bfc863d295f, whose defect is in `api/reporting/records._show_bug`'s `claims_fix` regex: `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*(?:and\s+)?ID` requires a comma after every list element, so the last id of an "and"-joined fix list never matches. The diff provided here does not touch `api/reporting/records.py` at all — it only rewrites the fix-list parsing in `kind_worklog.py` (and references a different bug id, `Bf228d082de`). Concretely, given a record whose text is `fixes bugs A1 and X` or `fixes bugs A1, A2 and X`, `_show_bug` still runs the unchanged comma-requiring regex, returns no match for `X`, and the fix task is still reported under `mentioned_by` rather than as fixing `X`. The new regression test only exercises the worklog export path (`registry.render_body("worklog", ...)`) and therefore cannot fail on the unfixed `_show_bug` behavior — it would pass or fail entirely independently of the bug the change claims to close. As submitted, the change does not fix the reported bug and its test does not cover the reported probe.
