chunk_findings.detail: Changing the split pattern from `r",|\band\b"` to `r",|\s+and\s+"` makes the "and" separator require whitespace on *both* sides. That is fine for the canonical `A, B and X`, but it regresses any list where a comma is followed directly by `and` (or where `and` is adjacent to a comma/start with no leading space). Example: `_fixed_bugs("x (fixes bugs A,B,and X)")` now returns `["A", "B", "and X"]`, whereas the old regex returned `["A", "B", "X"]`. The real id `X` is silently dropped and a bogus id `and X` is emitted/exported; the same happens for `"A,and B"` (piece after the comma is `and B`, which has no leading whitespace to match `\s+and\s+`) and for `"A, B,and X"`. So for these inputs the parser reintroduces exactly the symptom the task set out to fix (X not recognized as fixed).

chunk_findings.detail: The replacement list pattern `(?:[\w-]+(?:\s*,\s*(?:and\s+)?|\s+and\s+))*` is ambiguous, because the optional `and\s+` inside the comma-alternative and the following iteration's `[\w-]+` both match a bare `and`. A task title such as `"T (fixes A" + ", and"*60 + " )"` therefore has exponentially many parses (each `and` can be consumed either as the trailing `and` of one separator or as the next word). Since the bug id never appears anywhere, `re` must exhaust every one of those parses before concluding no match; because `_show_bug` runs `claims_fix` over every task title for every `ddflow show <bug>`, that single title hangs the command. The pre-change pattern `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*` had no overlap between the per-iteration word and separator and matched in linear time, so this cost is newly introduced by the diff. (The functional cases in the new test — `A and X`, `A, B and X`, `A, B, and X` — do match correctly; the defect is the backtracking blow-up on the non-matching sibling.)

chunk_findings.detail: The new separator `r",|\s+and\s+"` requires whitespace on *both* sides of `and`, but the grammar this parser is supposed to mirror names `and` with only a trailing space requirement: `(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*(?:and\s+)?ID`. That regex accepts an `and` that follows a comma with no space, so `_FIXES` captures a list like `A,B,and X` as `A,B,and X`, but the splitter then cannot break `and X` off, because there is no `\s+` before `and`. Concretely, `_fixed_bugs("fixes bugs A,B,and X")` now returns `["A", "B", "and X"]` (a bogus id `and X` plus a lost `X`), whereas the previous pattern `\band\b` returned `["A", "B", "X"]`. So this change trades the hyphenated-id bug for a regression on the comma-without-space form of the very same "and"-joined list (e.g. terse commit subjects `fixes bugs A,B,and X`), and the failure is exactly the class of bug being fixed: `X` is again attributed to `mentioned_by` rather than fixing. The added test only covers the spaced variants (`A, B, and X`, `A and X`), so it does not catch this; a separator that tolerates a missing leading space (e.g. `r",|\band\b(?![\w-])"` with a guard for `-and-`, or splitting on `\s*,\s*|\s+and\s+` while first protecting hyphenated ids) would cover both cases.

chunk_findings.detail: The change only rewrites the *separator* regex that `re.split` runs over `m.group(1)` — i.e. over the fix list that `_FIXES` has **already captured**. The defect quoted in the bug report is a *match* regex (`(?:[\w-]+\s*,\s*)*(?:and\s+)?ID`) that bounds how much of the title is captured as the fix list; `_FIXES` is not touched by this diff, so it can still stop capturing before the `and X` tail. Concretely, for the two titles the report names as failing — `x (fixes bugs A, B and X)` and `x (fixes bugs A and X)` — the new pattern `,\s*(?:and\s+)?|\s+and\s+` produces exactly the same split as the old `,|\s+and\s+` (the old alternative `\s+and\s+` already consumed the `" and "`), which is why the pre-existing, unchanged assertions in tests/test_export_worklog_fix_list.py:56–57 already expect `["A","B","X"]` and `["A","X"]` and pass. If X is dropped in practice it was never captured by `_FIXES`, and no rewrite of the separator can re-introduce a token the match never captured. The two added assertions instead cover a different input class (`A,B,and X`, `A,and B-and-c`) where a comma is glued to `and`; they are green both pre/post for the reported titles, so the regression test never exercises the failure described in the bug. chunk_findings.detail: The clamp fixes the reported direction (a trailing `]` after the id's closing `]` made depth negative and swallowed the following separator) but trades it for the opposite failure for any single node id whose param value contains two `]` and then a comma inside the id's brackets. `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]")` — the node id for `@pytest.mark.parametrize("s", ["a]b]c,d"])` — traces as: `[`→1, `]`→0, second `]`→`max(0,-1)=0`, then `,` is seen at depth 0 and splits, returning `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c", "d]"]`. Under the old code the second `]` drove depth to -1, so the `,` was kept and the function returned the single entry `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]"]` — which is the correct parse (the comma is inside the id's brackets). The clamped version therefore rejects a regression test that actually exists: `_unresolved_tests` will check `tests/a.py::test[a]b]c` and `d]`, find neither, and report the valid node id as missing. This is the mirror image of the bug being fixed, so the `max(0, ...)` heuristic is only sound when the deeper `]` is the id's final character; it needs the same treatment its sibling `_looks_like_several` gets or a bracket-count that is not reset by an in-value `]`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py `_split_outside_brackets` (the `depth = max(0, ...)` line)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic decides a `]` closes the parametrize id's brackets whenever the next character is `""`, `,`, `;` or whitespace. But the whole reason for this bug is that a parametrize value may itself contain `]`, and such a value may also contain `,`/`;` (the sibling test `tests/a.py::t[1,2;3]` already asserts commas/semicolons inside brackets must not split). When the embedded `]` is immediately followed by a separator, the code wrongly treats it as the closing bracket.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b]")`. Tracing line 86-88: at `[`, `inside=True`; the `a` is appended; at the first `]`, `spec[i+1]` is `','`, so `after in ",;"` is true and `inside` is set to `False`; the following `,` then hits `if ch in ",;" and not inside` and splits. The call returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]']` (and the two-entry list `"tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/b.py::u"` returns three entries `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]', 'tests/b.py::u']`) instead of the single entry `tests/a.py::t[a],b]`. This is structurally identical to the case the new test covers (`tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]`, where the embedded `]` happens to be followed by `b` rather than the comma): one `[`, two `]`, comma between them; the outcome flips purely on the character after the first `]`, so `t[a],b]` is split inside its own brackets while `t[a]b]c,d]` is not. A value like `t[a] b,c]` (embedded `]` followed by whitespace then a comma) fails the same way via `after.isspace()`. The result is a spurious extra entry (e.g. `b]`) that `_unresolved_tests` will see as a missing test, i.e. the same "missing test never resolved / wrong resolution" failure mode this change was meant to eliminate.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:86-88 (`_split_outside_brackets`)

chunk_findings.detail: Over-split: any bracketed parametrize value containing a comma followed by a token ending in `.py` is torn apart, even though the comma is inside the id's brackets. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]")`: after `[` `bracketed=True`, every `,`/`;` is tested against `_NEXT_PATH.match(spec, i+1)`; at the comma the remainder is `b.py]`, which the regex matches (`[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` matches `.py`, `(?![\w.])` sees `]`), so it splits. The function returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b.py]']` instead of the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]']`. This is exactly the case the new test `test_a_value_whose_inner_bracket_meets_a_separator_stays_one_entry` covers for `t[a],b]` — it only passes because `b]` lacks the `.py`; the sibling input `t[a.py,b.py]` fails the same way (returns `['tests/a.py::t[a.py', 'b.py]']`). The pre-change code (comma suppressed while `inside`) returned one entry here, so this is a regression introduced by the diff, and the new tests do not exercise a value token ending in `.py`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:_split_outside_brackets (`_NEXT_PATH` + `bracketed` condition)

chunk_findings.detail: Under-split: once an entry is bracketed, a following separator is ignored unless the next entry starts with a file path, so a legitimate non-path entry is merged. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x")`: at the comma `bracketed=True` and the remainder ` pytest -k x` contains no `.py`, so no split; the result is the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x']`. The function's own contract ("entries separated by ',' or ';'") and the newly added `test_entries_without_brackets_split_as_before` treat `pytest -k x` as a separate entry (it splits there only because no `[` preceded it), so the behavior is inconsistent and the command is swallowed into the node id, which is the same failure mode (an entry that is never seen as its own item) that this change set out to fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:_split_outside_brackets (`_NEXT_PATH` + `bracketed` condition)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_closes_unopened` scans the *entire* remainder `spec[i+1:]`, which includes the following entries, so an unbalanced `]` inside the *second* entry's parametrize value is misread as "closing a bracket the current entry never opened", and the split is suppressed.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]")`.

- At the comma, `cur == "tests/a.py::t[x]"` ends with `]` (first condition passes).
- `rest == "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"`. Walking it: `[` → depth 1, the first `]` → depth 0, then the trailing `]` → depth −1, so `_closes_unopened` returns `True`.
- The `and not _closes_unopened(...)` term is therefore `False`, the separator is appended to `cur`, and the function returns the single entry `["tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]` instead of the two entries `["tests/a.py::t[x]", "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]`.

The docstring itself declares `t[x]y]` a legitimate parametrize id, so `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is a valid second entry (its value is `a]b`). Because the list is not split, `_unresolved_tests` only looks at `tests/a.py::t` and the genuinely missing `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is never flagged — precisely the failure mode Bfc9daca269 is supposed to close, still reachable whenever the second bracketed entry's value contains a `]`. The added test only covers a second entry with balanced brackets (`tests/c.py::d[e]`), so it does not exercise this case.

Note this is a regression relative to the removed `_NEXT_PATH` approach, which matched the second entry by its leading `… .py` token and split correctly here.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py (_split_outside_brackets / _closes_unopened)

chunk_findings.detail:
Input: `tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]`.

This is a single node id whose value is `a],b.py,c` (the documented shape `t[a],b]` generalised, i.e. the separator before `]` is inside the id, and the rest `b.py,c]` closes a `]` it never opened). On the *old* code the first comma sees `cur == "tests/x.py::t[a]"` (ends with `]`), and `_closes_unopened("b.py,c]")` is `True`, so the branch is not taken and the spec is correctly kept as one entry.

On the *new* code `_NEXT_PATH.match("b.py,c]", 0)` succeeds: `[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` consumes `.py`, and the lookahead `(?=::|[\s,;]|$)` matches the following `,`. So the entry is split at the first comma, `bracketed` is reset to `False`, and the remaining comma (now "outside brackets") splits again. The function returns three entries:

    ["tests/x.py::t[a]", "b.py", "c]"]   # after
    ["tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]"]         # before (correct)

`b.py` here is a fragment of the parametrize value, not a following test path, so `_unresolved_tests` now resolves bogus entries (`b.py`, `c]`) instead of the real one. The asymmetry is visible in the regex's own comment: `t[a],b.py]` is handled (the `]` is not in the lookahead set), but `t[a],b.py,c]` / `t[a],b.py::c]` are not — the new "a test path follows" reason overrides `_closes_unopened` even when the following `.py` token is a value rather than an entry.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:_split_outside_brackets (the `_NEXT_PATH.match(...) or ...` clause)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_malformed` encodes the assumption "a node id's parametrize part is its LAST part", so it flags any entry that contains `[` but does not end in `]`. Pytest node ids violate this for class-level parametrization: a class decorated with `pytest.mark.parametrize` produces ids of the form `tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m` (the parametrize bracket sits on the class, followed by `::method`), so such an id is a *valid, well-formed* node id but `_malformed` returns `True` for it. This makes the global minimum prefer merging a list that should split. Concretely, for

    spec = "tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m,tests/b.py::test_n[y]"

the only separator is the comma. Cutting there gives entries `"tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m"` (flagged malformed → 1) and `"tests/b.py::test_n[y]"` (valid → 0), i.e. `(1, -2, …)`. Not cutting gives the single entry `"tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m,tests/b.py::test_n[y]"`, which ends in `]` with `[` before it, so it is *not* flagged, i.e. `(0, -1, …)`. The `min` picks the fewer-malformed single entry, so `_split_outside_brackets` returns one entry even though there are two perfectly well-formed readings — directly violating the design's own rule that a genuinely ambiguous, well-formed input must resolve to *more* entries. The second test is then never checked on its own, which is the same failure mode the change was supposed to fix for `'tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'`; it just moves the trigger to any list whose first element is a class-parametrized node id and whose second element ends in `]`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py: `_malformed` / `_split_outside_brackets`

chunk_findings.detail:
Given `spec = "tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"` (a real parametrize id `[a],b`, i.e. the inner list `[a]` plus a comma, wrapped by pytest's outer `[...]`):

- Trace of the new code: `[` → `inside=True`; `[` → `inside=True`; `]` with `after=","` → `inside = not True = False`; then `,` is seen while `not inside` → the string is split at the comma; the trailing `]` is ignored because `inside` is already `False`.
- Actual result: `["tests/a.py::t[[a]", "b]"]` — one node id became two fragments.
- Correct result (and what the *removed* clamped code produced): `["tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"]`. Under the old code `[[` drove `depth` to 2, the interior `]` decremented it to 1 (still > 0), so the comma inside the brackets did not split; the final `]` closed it correctly.

So this change regresses inputs that the clamped version handled. The comma here is inside the outer bracket, so `_unresolved_tests` will now receive the bogus fragment `tests/a.py::t[[a]` and fail to match the actual test — the same class of failure (a valid entry not resolved / a non-existent test reported) that Bfc9daca269 is about. The same happens for an interior `]` followed by whitespace, e.g. `"tests/a.py::t[[a] b,c]"` → `["tests/a.py::t[[a] b", "c]"]`.

The added test only exercises interior `]` followed by `]` (`t[[1]]`) or by a non-separator, so it never hits the `after in ",;" or after.isspace()` path on an interior bracket that still has a matching `]` later.
chunk_findings.title: `_split_outside_brackets` (ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py, the `elif ch == "]" and inside:` branch, ~line 80–86)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic only splits a bracketed entry when the text following the separator never makes the bracket depth negative, and `_closes_unopened` scans the *entire remaining string* — including later entries. A later entry whose parametrize id itself contains an unmatched `]` therefore cancels an otherwise legitimate split, merging the whole list into one entry. This is exactly the shape the module documents/test as valid (`t[a],b]`, `t[x]y]`) and it reproduces bug Bfc9daca269.

Concretely, `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d],e]")`:

- at the comma after `t[a]`, `cur` ends in `]`, but `_closes_unopened("b],tests/c.py::d],e]")` hits the `]` after `b` and returns True → no split;
- at the comma after `t[a],b]`, `cur` ends in `]`, but `_closes_unopened("tests/c.py::d],e]")` hits the `]` after `d` and returns True → no split again.

Result: `["tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d],e]"]` (one entry), whereas the correct answer is `["tests/a.py::t[a],b]", "tests/c.py::d],e]"]`. The pre-change code split here, because `_NEXT_PATH` matched `tests/c.py` after the second comma, so this is a behavioral regression introduced by the change, not a pre-existing limitation. Note the added test `("tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d[e]", ...)` deliberately uses a *balanced* second id (`d[e]`), which is why it passes; the `d],e]` variant (a value holding `]` and `,`, explicitly listed as supported in the docstring) fails. The same root cause also blocks a split when a command following a bracketed id contains a `]` (e.g. `tests/a.py::t[x], pytest -k "a]b"`).

Because the missing second node id is never separated, `_unresolved_tests` again evaluates it as part of the first token, so a nonexistent regression test can be accepted — the very failure Bfc9daca269 intends to fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:81 (`_split_outside_brackets`, the new bracketed-split condition)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `_NEXT_PATH` disjunct is OR-ed ahead of the `_closes_unopened` guard, so a `.py`-looking token after a `]` forces a split even when the rest closes a bracket the entry never opened (i.e. even when the comma is provably inside a parametrize id, the case `_closes_unopened` exists to protect). Input:

    _split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b.py,c]")

At the first comma `cur` is `tests/a.py::t[a]` (ends with `]`) and the rest is `b.py,c]`; `_NEXT_PATH` matches `b.py` because `.py` is followed by `,` (in the `[\s,;]` lookahead). So it splits, `bracketed` resets to `False`, and the second comma splits again via the `not bracketed` branch, yielding three entries `["tests/a.py::t[a]", "b.py", "c]"]`. The docstring this diff touches explicitly promises that a parametrize value may hold `]` and `,` (`t[a],b]` is one value); the old condition kept this as the single entry `tests/a.py::t[a],b.py,c]` because `_closes_unopened("b.py,c]")` is true and blocks the split. chunk_findings.detail: The clamp fixes the reported direction (a trailing `]` after the id's closing `]` made depth negative and swallowed the following separator) but trades it for the opposite failure for any single node id whose param value contains two `]` and then a comma inside the id's brackets. `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]")` — the node id for `@pytest.mark.parametrize("s", ["a]b]c,d"])` — traces as: `[`→1, `]`→0, second `]`→`max(0,-1)=0`, then `,` is seen at depth 0 and splits, returning `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c", "d]"]`. Under the old code the second `]` drove depth to -1, so the `,` was kept and the function returned the single entry `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]"]` — which is the correct parse (the comma is inside the id's brackets). The clamped version therefore rejects a regression test that actually exists: `_unresolved_tests` will check `tests/a.py::test[a]b]c` and `d]`, find neither, and report the valid node id as missing. This is the mirror image of the bug being fixed, so the `max(0, ...)` heuristic is only sound when the deeper `]` is the id's final character; it needs the same treatment its sibling `_looks_like_several` gets or a bracket-count that is not reset by an in-value `]`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic decides a `]` closes the parametrize id's brackets whenever the next character is `""`, `,`, `;` or whitespace. But the whole reason for this bug is that a parametrize value may itself contain `]`, and such a value may also contain `,`/`;` (the sibling test `tests/a.py::t[1,2;3]` already asserts commas/semicolons inside brackets must not split). When the embedded `]` is immediately followed by a separator, the code wrongly treats it as the closing bracket.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b]")`. Tracing line 86-88: at `[`, `inside=True`; the `a` is appended; at the first `]`, `spec[i+1]` is `','`, so `after in ",;"` is true and `inside` is set to `False`; the following `,` then hits `if ch in ",;" and not inside` and splits. The call returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]']` (and the two-entry list `"tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/b.py::u"` returns three entries `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]', 'tests/b.py::u']`) instead of the single entry `tests/a.py::t[a],b]`. This is structurally identical to the case the new test covers (`tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]`, where the embedded `]` happens to be followed by `b` rather than the comma): one `[`, two `]`, comma between them; the outcome flips purely on the character after the first `]`, so `t[a],b]` is split inside its own brackets while `t[a]b]c,d]` is not. A value like `t[a] b,c]` (embedded `]` followed by whitespace then a comma) fails the same way via `after.isspace()`. The result is a spurious extra entry (e.g. `b]`) that `_unresolved_tests` will see as a missing test, i.e. the same "missing test never resolved / wrong resolution" failure mode this change was meant to eliminate.

chunk_findings.detail: Over-split: any bracketed parametrize value containing a comma followed by a token ending in `.py` is torn apart, even though the comma is inside the id's brackets. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]")`: after `[` `bracketed=True`, every `,`/`;` is tested against `_NEXT_PATH.match(spec, i+1)`; at the comma the remainder is `b.py]`, which the regex matches (`[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` matches `.py`, `(?![\w.])` sees `]`), so it splits. The function returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b.py]']` instead of the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]']`. This is exactly the case the new test `test_a_value_whose_inner_bracket_meets_a_separator_stays_one_entry` covers for `t[a],b]` — it only passes because `b]` lacks the `.py`; the sibling input `t[a.py,b.py]` fails the same way (returns `['tests/a.py::t[a.py', 'b.py]']`). The pre-change code (comma suppressed while `inside`) returned one entry here, so this is a regression introduced by the diff, and the new tests do not exercise a value token ending in `.py`.

chunk_findings.detail: Under-split: once an entry is bracketed, a following separator is ignored unless the next entry starts with a file path, so a legitimate non-path entry is merged. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x")`: at the comma `bracketed=True` and the remainder ` pytest -k x` contains no `.py`, so no split; the result is the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x']`. The function's own contract ("entries separated by ',' or ';'") and the newly added `test_entries_without_brackets_split_as_before` treat `pytest -k x` as a separate entry (it splits there only because no `[` preceded it), so the behavior is inconsistent and the command is swallowed into the node id, which is the same failure mode (an entry that is never seen as its own item) that this change set out to fix.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_closes_unopened` scans the *entire* remainder `spec[i+1:]`, which includes the following entries, so an unbalanced `]` inside the *second* entry's parametrize value is misread as "closing a bracket the current entry never opened", and the split is suppressed.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]")`.

- At the comma, `cur == "tests/a.py::t[x]"` ends with `]` (first condition passes).
- `rest == "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"`. Walking it: `[` → depth 1, the first `]` → depth 0, then the trailing `]` → depth −1, so `_closes_unopened` returns `True`.
- The `and not _closes_unopened(...)` term is therefore `False`, the separator is appended to `cur`, and the function returns the single entry `["tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]` instead of the two entries `["tests/a.py::t[x]", "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]`.

The docstring itself declares `t[x]y]` a legitimate parametrize id, so `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is a valid second entry (its value is `a]b`). Because the list is not split, `_unresolved_tests` only looks at `tests/a.py::t` and the genuinely missing `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is never flagged — precisely the failure mode Bfc9daca269 is supposed to close, still reachable whenever the second bracketed entry's value contains a `]`. The added test only covers a second entry with balanced brackets (`tests/c.py::d[e]`), so it does not exercise this case.

Note this is a regression relative to the removed `_NEXT_PATH` approach, which matched the second entry by its leading `… .py` token and split correctly here.

chunk_findings.detail:
Input: `tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]`.

This is a single node id whose value is `a],b.py,c` (the documented shape `t[a],b]` generalised, i.e. the separator before `]` is inside the id, and the rest `b.py,c]` closes a `]` it never opened). On the *old* code the first comma sees `cur == "tests/x.py::t[a]"` (ends with `]`), and `_closes_unopened("b.py,c]")` is `True`, so the branch is not taken and the spec is correctly kept as one entry.

On the *new* code `_NEXT_PATH.match("b.py,c]", 0)` succeeds: `[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` consumes `.py`, and the lookahead `(?=::|[\s,;]|$)` matches the following `,`. So the entry is split at the first comma, `bracketed` is reset to `False`, and the remaining comma (now "outside brackets") splits again. The function returns three entries:

    ["tests/x.py::t[a]", "b.py", "c]"]   # after
    ["tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]"]         # before (correct)

`b.py` here is a fragment of the parametrize value, not a following test path, so `_unresolved_tests` now resolves bogus entries (`b.py`, `c]`) instead of the real one. The asymmetry is visible in the regex's own comment: `t[a],b.py]` is handled (the `]` is not in the lookahead set), but `t[a],b.py,c]` / `t[a],b.py::c]` are not — the new "a test path follows" reason overrides `_closes_unopened` even when the following `.py` token is a value rather than an entry.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_malformed` encodes the assumption "a node id's parametrize part is its LAST part", so it flags any entry that contains `[` but does not end in `]`. Pytest node ids violate this for class-level parametrization: a class decorated with `pytest.mark.parametrize` produces ids of the form `tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m` (the parametrize bracket sits on the class, followed by `::method`), so such an id is a *valid, well-formed* node id but `_malformed` returns `True` for it. This makes the global minimum prefer merging a list that should split. Concretely, for

    spec = "tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m,tests/b.py::test_n[y]"

the only separator is the comma. Cutting there gives entries `"tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m"` (flagged malformed → 1) and `"tests/b.py::test_n[y]"` (valid → 0), i.e. `(1, -2, …)`. Not cutting gives the single entry `"tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m,tests/b.py::test_n[y]"`, which ends in `]` with `[` before it, so it is *not* flagged, i.e. `(0, -1, …)`. The `min` picks the fewer-malformed single entry, so `_split_outside_brackets` returns one entry even though there are two perfectly well-formed readings — directly violating the design's own rule that a genuinely ambiguous, well-formed input must resolve to *more* entries. The second test is then never checked on its own, which is the same failure mode the change was supposed to fix for `'tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'`; it just moves the trigger to any list whose first element is a class-parametrized node id and whose second element ends in `]`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new first clause exempts *any* piece that contains whitespace and doesn't itself start with a `....py::` path, which is broader than “a command”: a whitespace can also live inside a node id's parametrize value. Given `spec = "tests/a.py::t[a],hello world]"` — a single valid node id for a string parameter whose id is `a],hello world` (pytest keeps spaces in string ids; `_split_outside_brackets` is documented to handle params holding `]`, `[`, `,`, `;`, and space is no different) — the whole entry ends in `]` so `_malformed(whole)` is False, and the cut at the comma yields pieces `tests/a.py::t[a]` (well formed) and `hello world]`, which is also reported not malformed precisely because of the new whitespace clause. Both readings therefore have zero malformed entries, and the tie-break documented in the changed docstring (“the one with more entries wins”) makes `_split_outside_brackets` return `["tests/a.py::t[a]", "hello world]"]` — it splits one existing test id into a truncated id plus the garbage fragment `hello world]`. Before this change the old `_malformed` flagged `hello world]` (`]` with no `[`) as malformed, so the whole string was kept as a single well-formed entry and the real node id was resolvable; the added whitespace exemption is what introduces the wrong split, so a valid regression test is now reported unresolved (or a bogus `hello world]` test is looked up).

chunk_findings.detail:
Given `spec = "tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"` (a real parametrize id `[a],b`, i.e. the inner list `[a]` plus a comma, wrapped by pytest's outer `[...]`):

- Trace of the new code: `[` → `inside=True`; `[` → `inside=True`; `]` with `after=","` → `inside = not True = False`; then `,` is seen while `not inside` → the string is split at the comma; the trailing `]` is ignored because `inside` is already `False`.
- Actual result: `["tests/a.py::t[[a]", "b]"]` — one node id became two fragments.
- Correct result (and what the *removed* clamped code produced): `["tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"]`. Under the old code `[[` drove `depth` to 2, the interior `]` decremented it to 1 (still > 0), so the comma inside the brackets did not split; the final `]` closed it correctly.

So this change regresses inputs that the clamped version handled. The comma here is inside the outer bracket, so `_unresolved_tests` will now receive the bogus fragment `tests/a.py::t[[a]` and fail to match the actual test — the same class of failure (a valid entry not resolved / a non-existent test reported) that Bfc9daca269 is about. The same happens for an interior `]` followed by whitespace, e.g. `"tests/a.py::t[[a] b,c]"` → `["tests/a.py::t[[a] b", "c]"]`.

The added test only exercises interior `]` followed by `]` (`t[[1]]`) or by a non-separator, so it never hits the `after in ",;" or after.isspace()` path on an interior bracket that still has a matching `]` later.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic only splits a bracketed entry when the text following the separator never makes the bracket depth negative, and `_closes_unopened` scans the *entire remaining string* — including later entries. A later entry whose parametrize id itself contains an unmatched `]` therefore cancels an otherwise legitimate split, merging the whole list into one entry. This is exactly the shape the module documents/test as valid (`t[a],b]`, `t[x]y]`) and it reproduces bug Bfc9daca269.

Concretely, `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d],e]")`:

- at the comma after `t[a]`, `cur` ends in `]`, but `_closes_unopened("b],tests/c.py::d],e]")` hits the `]` after `b` and returns True → no split;
- at the comma after `t[a],b]`, `cur` ends in `]`, but `_closes_unopened("tests/c.py::d],e]")` hits the `]` after `d` and returns True → no split again.

Result: `["tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d],e]"]` (one entry), whereas the correct answer is `["tests/a.py::t[a],b]", "tests/c.py::d],e]"]`. The pre-change code split here, because `_NEXT_PATH` matched `tests/c.py` after the second comma, so this is a behavioral regression introduced by the change, not a pre-existing limitation. Note the added test `("tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d[e]", ...)` deliberately uses a *balanced* second id (`d[e]`), which is why it passes; the `d],e]` variant (a value holding `]` and `,`, explicitly listed as supported in the docstring) fails. The same root cause also blocks a split when a command following a bracketed id contains a `]` (e.g. `tests/a.py::t[x], pytest -k "a]b"`).

Because the missing second node id is never separated, `_unresolved_tests` again evaluates it as part of the first token, so a nonexistent regression test can be accepted — the very failure Bfc9daca269 intends to fix.

Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]")`: after `[` `bracketed=True`, every `,`/`;` is tested against `_NEXT_PATH.match(spec, i+1)`; at the comma the remainder is `b.py]`, which the regex matches (`[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` matches `.py`, `(?![\w.])` sees `]`), so it splits. The function returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b.py]']` instead of the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]']`. This is exactly the case the new test `test_a_value_whose_inner_bracket_meets_a_separator_stays_one_entry` covers for `t[a],b]` — it only passes because `b]` lacks the `.py`; the sibling input `t[a.py,b.py]` fails the same way (returns `['tests/a.py::t[a.py', 'b.py]']`). The pre-change code (comma suppressed while `inside`) returned one entry here, so this is a regression introduced by the diff, and the new tests do not exercise a value token ending in `.py`.

chunk_findings.detail: Under-split: once an entry is bracketed, a following separator is ignored unless the next entry starts with a file path, so a legitimate non-path entry is merged. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x")`: at the comma `bracketed=True` and the remainder ` pytest -k x` contains no `.py`, so no split; the result is the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x']`. The function's own contract ("entries separated by ',' or ';'") and the newly added `test_entries_without_brackets_split_as_before` treat `pytest -k x` as a separate entry (it splits there only because no `[` preceded it), so the behavior is inconsistent and the command is swallowed into the node id, which is the same failure mode (an entry that is never seen as its own item) that this change set out to fix.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_closes_unopened` scans the *entire* remainder `spec[i+1:]`, which includes the following entries, so an unbalanced `]` inside the *second* entry's parametrize value is misread as "closing a bracket the current entry never opened", and the split is suppressed.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]")`.

- At the comma, `cur == "tests/a.py::t[x]"` ends with `]` (first condition passes).
- `rest == "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"`. Walking it: `[` → depth 1, the first `]` → depth 0, then the trailing `]` → depth −1, so `_closes_unopened` returns `True`.
- The `and not _closes_unopened(...)` term is therefore `False`, the separator is appended to `cur`, and the function returns the single entry `["tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]` instead of the two entries `["tests/a.py::t[x]", "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]`.

The docstring itself declares `t[x]y]` a legitimate parametrize id, so `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is a valid second entry (its value is `a]b`). Because the list is not split, `_unresolved_tests` only looks at `tests/a.py::t` and the genuinely missing `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is never flagged — precisely the failure mode Bfc9daca269 is supposed to close, still reachable whenever the second bracketed entry's value contains a `]`. The added test only covers a second entry with balanced brackets (`tests/c.py::d[e]`), so it does not exercise this case.

Note this is a regression relative to the removed `_NEXT_PATH` approach, which matched the second entry by its leading `… .py` token and split correctly here.

chunk_findings.detail:
Input: `tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]`.

This is a single node id whose value is `a],b.py,c` (the documented shape `t[a],b]` generalised, i.e. the separator before `]` is inside the id, and the rest `b.py,c]` closes a `]` it never opened). On the *old* code the first comma sees `cur == "tests/x.py::t[a]"` (ends with `]`), and `_closes_unopened("b.py,c]")` is `True`, so the branch is not taken and the spec is correctly kept as one entry.

On the *new* code `_NEXT_PATH.match("b.py,c]", 0)` succeeds: `[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` consumes `.py`, and the lookahead `(?=::|[\s,;]|$)` matches the following `,`. So the entry is split at the first comma, `bracketed` is reset to `False`, and the remaining comma (now "outside brackets") splits again. The function returns three entries:

    ["tests/x.py::t[a]", "b.py", "c]"]   # after
    ["tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]"]         # before (correct)

`b.py` here is a fragment of the parametrize value, not a following test path, so `_unresolved_tests` now resolves bogus entries (`b.py`, `c]`) instead of the real one. The asymmetry is visible in the regex's own comment: `t[a],b.py]` is handled (the `]` is not in the lookahead set), but `t[a],b.py,c]` / `t[a],b.py::c]` are not — the new "a test path follows" reason overrides `_closes_unopened` even when the following `.py` token is a value rather than an entry.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_malformed` encodes the assumption "a node id's parametrize part is its LAST part", so it flags any entry that contains `[` but does not end in `]`. Pytest node ids violate this for class-level parametrization: a class decorated with `pytest.mark.parametrize` produces ids of the form `tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m` (the parametrize bracket sits on the class, followed by `::method`), so such an id is a *valid, well-formed* node id but `_malformed` returns `True` for it. This makes the global minimum prefer merging a list that should split. Concretely, for

    spec = "tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m,tests/b.py::test_n[y]"

the only separator is the comma. Cutting there gives entries `"tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m"` (flagged malformed → 1) and `"tests/b.py::test_n[y]"` (valid → 0), i.e. `(1, -2, …)`. Not cutting gives the single entry `"tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m,tests/b.py::test_n[y]"`, which ends in `]` with `[` before it, so it is *not* flagged, i.e. `(0, -1, …)`. The `min` picks the fewer-malformed single entry, so `_split_outside_brackets` returns one entry even though there are two perfectly well-formed readings — directly violating the design's own rule that a genuinely ambiguous, well-formed input must resolve to *more* entries. The second test is then never checked on its own, which is the same failure mode the change was supposed to fix for `'tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'`; it just moves the trigger to any list whose first element is a class-parametrized node id and whose second element ends in `]`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new first clause exempts *any* piece that contains whitespace and doesn't itself start with a `....py::` path, which is broader than “a command”: a whitespace can also live inside a node id's parametrize value. Given `spec = "tests/a.py::t[a],hello world]"` — a single valid node id for a string parameter whose id is `a],hello world` (pytest keeps spaces in string ids; `_split_outside_brackets` is documented to handle params holding `]`, `[`, `,`, `;`, and space is no different) — the whole entry ends in `]` so `_malformed(whole)` is False, and the cut at the comma yields pieces `tests/a.py::t[a]` (well formed) and `hello world]`, which is also reported not malformed precisely because of the new whitespace clause. Both readings therefore have zero malformed entries, and the tie-break documented in the changed docstring (“the one with more entries wins”) makes `_split_outside_brackets` return `["tests/a.py::t[a]", "hello world]"]` — it splits one existing test id into a truncated id plus the garbage fragment `hello world]`. Before this change the old `_malformed` flagged `hello world]` (`]` with no `[`) as malformed, so the whole string was kept as a single well-formed entry and the real node id was resolvable; the added whitespace exemption is what introduces the wrong split, so a valid regression test is now reported unresolved (or a bogus `hello world]` test is looked up).

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug (Bfc9daca269) lives in `_split_outside_brackets`, and that function is never touched by this diff — the only production hunks are in `_unresolved_tests` and the new `_bare_names`/`_PARAMS`. So the probe from the intent still fails: `_split_outside_brackets('tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2')` sees depth 1 at `[`, back to 0 at the `]` after `x`, still 0 through `y`, then `]` drives it to −1; the following comma is at depth −1, not 0, so no split happens and the call still returns the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2']`. The new `_bare_names` does not compensate: for `names = 't[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'` the regex `\[.*?\](?=::|\s|$)` finds no `]` followed by `::`/whitespace/EOS, so it falls through to `bare.split('[', 1)[0]`, yielding `['t']` — `_unresolved_tests` still only verifies `tests/a.py::t` and never resolves `tests/missing.py::t2`, i.e. the invalid regression test is still accepted.

chunk_findings.detail: The test that is supposed to guard the intent's fix cannot fail on the unfixed code. Its input `"tests/a.py::t[a],tests/b.py::u[x]]"` puts the comma at bracket depth 0: `[a]` opens and closes before the comma, so even the unclamped `depth += {'[':1,']':-1}` splitter still hits depth 0 at that comma and returns the two expected entries. The negative-depth condition the bug is about (a `]` inside the id *before* the comma, as in `t[x]y],...`) never occurs here — the extra `]` in `u[x]]` sits after the comma and can only affect a later comma, of which there is none. A regression test that actually fails on the unfixed code needs the comma met while depth is already negative, e.g. `"tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/b.py::u"`, which the added test does not do, so `ddflow complete ... --regression-test` would close the bug on a test that passes either way.

chunk_findings.detail:
Given `spec = "tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"` (a real parametrize id `[a],b`, i.e. the inner list `[a]` plus a comma, wrapped by pytest's outer `[...]`):

- Trace of the new code: `[` → `inside=True`; `[` → `inside=True`; `]` with `after=","` → `inside = not True = False`; then `,` is seen while `not inside` → the string is split at the comma; the trailing `]` is ignored because `inside` is already `False`.
- Actual result: `["tests/a.py::t[[a]", "b]"]` — one node id became two fragments.
- Correct result (and what the *removed* clamped code produced): `["tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"]`. Under the old code `[[` drove `depth` to 2, the interior `]` decremented it to 1 (still > 0), so the comma inside the brackets did not split; the final `]` closed it correctly.

So this change regresses inputs that the clamped version handled. The comma here is inside the outer bracket, so `_unresolved_tests` will now receive the bogus fragment `tests/a.py::t[[a]` and fail to match the actual test — the same class of failure (a valid entry not resolved / a non-existent test reported) that Bfc9daca269 is about. The same happens for an interior `]` followed by whitespace, e.g. `"tests/a.py::t[[a] b,c]"` → `["tests/a.py::t[[a] b", "c]"]`.

The added test only exercises interior `]` followed by `]` (`t[[1]]`) or by a non-separator, so it never hits the `after in ",;" or after.isspace()` path on an interior bracket that still has a matching `]` later.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic only splits a bracketed entry when the text following the separator never makes the bracket depth negative, and `_closes_unopened` scans the *entire remaining string* — including later entries. A later entry whose parametrize id itself contains an unmatched `]` therefore cancels an otherwise legitimate split, merging the whole list into one entry. This is exactly the shape the module documents/test as valid (`t[a],b]`, `t[x]y]`) and it reproduces bug Bfc9daca269.

Concretely, `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d],e]")`:

- at the comma after `t[a]`, `cur` ends in `]`, but `_closes_unopened("b],tests/c.py::d],e]")` hits the `]` after `b` and returns True → no split;
- at the comma after `t[a],b]`, `cur` ends in `]`, but `_closes_unopened("tests/c.py::d],e]")` hits the `]` after `d` and returns True → no split again.

Result: `["tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d],e]"]` (one entry), whereas the correct answer is `["tests/a.py::t[a],b]", "tests/c.py::d],e]"]`. The pre-change code split here, because `_NEXT_PATH` matched `tests/c.py` after the second comma, so this is a behavioral regression introduced by the change, not a pre-existing limitation. Note the added test `("tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d[e]", ...)` deliberately uses a *balanced* second id (`d[e]`), which is why it passes; the `d],e]` variant (a value holding `]` and `,`, explicitly listed as supported in the docstring) fails. The same root cause also blocks a split when a command following a bracketed id contains a `]` (e.g. `tests/a.py::t[x], pytest -k "a]b"`).

Because the missing second node id is never separated, `_unresolved_tests` again evaluates it as part of the first token, so a nonexistent regression test can be accepted — the very failure Bfc9daca269 intends to fix.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `_NEXT_PATH` disjunct is OR-ed ahead of the `_closes_unopened` guard, so a `.py`-looking token after a `]` forces a split even when the rest closes a bracket the entry never opened (i.e. even when the comma is provably inside a parametrize id, the case `_closes_unopened` exists to protect). Input:

    _split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b.py,c]")

At the first comma `cur` is `tests/a.py::t[a]` (ends with `]`) and the rest is `b.py,c]`; `_NEXT_PATH` matches `b.py` because `.py` is followed by `,` (in the `[\s,;]` lookahead). So it splits, `bracketed` resets to `False`, and the second comma splits again via the `not bracketed` branch, yielding three entries `["tests/a.py::t[a]", "b.py", "c]"]`. The docstring this diff touches explicitly promises that a parametrize value may hold `]` and `,` (`t[a],b]` is one value); the old condition kept this as the single entry `tests/a.py::t[a],b.py,c]` because `_closes_unopened("b.py,c]")` is true and blocks the split. So a single bracketed id whose value contains a `.py` token followed by a separator is now shredded into spurious "test" entries, which then feed `_unresolved_tests` — exactly the failure class (wrong number of parsed tests) the change is meant to eliminate. The added regression cases all place the `.py` path after a separator that is *between* entries, so they do not cover this shape; e.g. `tests/a.py::t[a],b.py::c]` (rest `b.py::c]`) also matches `_NEXT_PATH` and splits a single id.

chunk_findings.detail: `_PARAMS = re.compile(r"\[.*?\](?=::|\s|$)", re.S)` ends a parametrize id at the *nearest* `]` that is followed by `::`, whitespace or end-of-string. That lookahead is exactly the invariant B-bfu-param-sep documents as legal content inside an id ("`::` and `,` are legal inside `[...]`"). When an id contains `]` immediately before `::`, the regex mistakes the interior `]` for the id's terminator and strips only part of the id. Concrete input: `_bare_names("TestC::test_m[x]::y]")` (a valid pytest node id for `tests/test_a.py::TestC::test_m` parametrized with `ids=["x]::y"]`). The regex matches `[x]` (the `]` is followed by `::`), so `_PARAMS.sub` yields `"TestC::test_m::y]"`, and the function returns `['TestC', 'test_m', 'y]']` instead of the documented `['TestC', 'test_m']` — a spurious name `y]` is emitted that no test defines, so `_unresolved_tests` will treat a legitimate node id as unresolved/missing. This is a regression introduced by the change: the previous `names.split("[", 1)[0].split("::")` cut at the first `[` and produced `['TestC', 'test_m']` here, i.e. accepted the same id. The function's own docstring promises "every parametrize id removed", which this input violates.

chunk_findings.detail: The clamp fixes the reported direction (a trailing `]` after the id's closing `]` made depth negative and swallowed the following separator) but trades it for the opposite failure for any single node id whose param value contains two `]` and then a comma inside the id's brackets. `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]")` — the node id for `@pytest.mark.parametrize("s", ["a]b]c,d"])` — traces as: `[`→1, `]`→0, second `]`→`max(0,-1)=0`, then `,` is seen at depth 0 and splits, returning `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c", "d]"]`. Under the old code the second `]` drove depth to -1, so the `,` was kept and the function returned the single entry `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]"]` — which is the correct parse (the comma is inside the id's brackets). The clamped version therefore rejects a regression test that actually exists: `_unresolved_tests` will check `tests/a.py::test[a]b]c` and `d]`, find neither, and report the valid node id as missing. This is the mirror image of the bug being fixed, so the `max(0, ...)` heuristic is only sound when the deeper `]` is the id's final character; it needs the same treatment its sibling `_looks_like_several` gets or a bracket-count that is not reset by an in-value `]`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic decides a `]` closes the parametrize id's brackets whenever the next character is `""`, `,`, `;` or whitespace. But the whole reason for this bug is that a parametrize value may itself contain `]`, and such a value may also contain `,`/`;` (the sibling test `tests/a.py::t[1,2;3]` already asserts commas/semicolons inside brackets must not split). When the embedded `]` is immediately followed by a separator, the code wrongly treats it as the closing bracket.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b]")`. Tracing line 86-88: at `[`, `inside=True`; the `a` is appended; at the first `]`, `spec[i+1]` is `','`, so `after in ",;"` is true and `inside` is set to `False`; the following `,` then hits `if ch in ",;" and not inside` and splits. The call returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]']` (and the two-entry list `"tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/b.py::u"` returns three entries `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]', 'tests/b.py::u']`) instead of the single entry `tests/a.py::t[a],b]`. This is structurally identical to the case the new test covers (`tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]`, where the embedded `]` happens to be followed by `b` rather than the comma): one `[`, two `]`, comma between them; the outcome flips purely on the character after the first `]`, so `t[a],b]` is split inside its own brackets while `t[a]b]c,d]` is not. A value like `t[a] b,c]` (embedded `]` followed by whitespace then a comma) fails the same way via `after.isspace()`. The result is a spurious extra entry (e.g. `b]`) that `_unresolved_tests` will see as a missing test, i.e. the same "missing test never resolved / wrong resolution" failure mode this change was meant to eliminate.

- `rest == "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"`. Walking it: `[` → depth 1, the first `]` → depth 0, then the trailing `]` → depth −1, so `_closes_unopened` returns `True`.

chunk_findings.detail:
Input: `tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]`.

This is a single node id whose value is `a],b.py,c` (the documented shape `t[a],b]` generalised, i.e. the separator before `]` is inside the id, and the rest `b.py,c]` closes a `]` it never opened). On the *old* code the first comma sees `cur == "tests/x.py::t[a]"` (ends with `]`), and `_closes_unopened("b.py,c]")` is `True`, so the branch is not taken and the spec is correctly kept as one entry.

On the *new* code `_NEXT_PATH.match("b.py,c]", 0)` succeeds: `[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` consumes `.py`, and the lookahead `(?=::|[\s,;]|$)` matches the following `,`. So the entry is split at the first comma, `bracketed` is reset to `False`, and the remaining comma (now "outside brackets") splits again. The function returns three entries:

    ["tests/x.py::t[a]", "b.py", "c]"]   # after
    ["tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]"]         # before (correct)

`b.py` here is a fragment of the parametrize value, not a following test path, so `_unresolved_tests` now resolves bogus entries (`b.py`, `c]`) instead of the real one. The asymmetry is visible in the regex's own comment: `t[a],b.py]` is handled (the `]` is not in the lookahead set), but `t[a],b.py,c]` / `t[a],b.py::c]` are not — the new "a test path follows" reason overrides `_closes_unopened` even when the following `.py` token is a value rather than an entry.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_malformed` encodes the assumption "a node id's parametrize part is its LAST part", so it flags any entry that contains `[` but does not end in `]`. Pytest node ids violate this for class-level parametrization: a class decorated with `pytest.mark.parametrize` produces ids of the form `tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m` (the parametrize bracket sits on the class, followed by `::method`), so such an id is a *valid, well-formed* node id but `_malformed` returns `True` for it. This makes the global minimum prefer merging a list that should split. Concretely, for

    spec = "tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m,tests/b.py::test_n[y]"

the only separator is the comma. Cutting there gives entries `"tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m"` (flagged malformed → 1) and `"tests/b.py::test_n[y]"` (valid → 0), i.e. `(1, -2, …)`. Not cutting gives the single entry `"tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m,tests/b.py::test_n[y]"`, which ends in `]` with `[` before it, so it is *not* flagged, i.e. `(0, -1, …)`. The `min` picks the fewer-malformed single entry, so `_split_outside_brackets` returns one entry even though there are two perfectly well-formed readings — directly violating the design's own rule that a genuinely ambiguous, well-formed input must resolve to *more* entries. The second test is then never checked on its own, which is the same failure mode the change was supposed to fix for `'tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'`; it just moves the trigger to any list whose first element is a class-parametrized node id and whose second element ends in `]`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new first clause exempts *any* piece that contains whitespace and doesn't itself start with a `....py::` path, which is broader than “a command”: a whitespace can also live inside a node id's parametrize value. Given `spec = "tests/a.py::t[a],hello world]"` — a single valid node id for a string parameter whose id is `a],hello world` (pytest keeps spaces in string ids; `_split_outside_brackets` is documented to handle params holding `]`, `[`, `,`, `;`, and space is no different) — the whole entry ends in `]` so `_malformed(whole)` is False, and the cut at the comma yields pieces `tests/a.py::t[a]` (well formed) and `hello world]`, which is also reported not malformed precisely because of the new whitespace clause. Both readings therefore have zero malformed entries, and the tie-break documented in the changed docstring (“the one with more entries wins”) makes `_split_outside_brackets` return `["tests/a.py::t[a]", "hello world]"]` — it splits one existing test id into a truncated id plus the garbage fragment `hello world]`. Before this change the old `_malformed` flagged `hello world]` (`]` with no `[`) as malformed, so the whole string was kept as a single well-formed entry and the real node id was resolvable; the added whitespace exemption is what introduces the wrong split, so a valid regression test is now reported unresolved (or a bogus `hello world]` test is looked up).

So the probe from the intent still fails: `_split_outside_brackets('tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2')` sees depth 1 at `[`, back to 0 at the `]` after `x`, still 0 through `y`, then `]` drives it to −1; the following comma is at depth −1, not 0, so no split happens and the call still returns the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2']`. The new `_bare_names` does not compensate: for `names = 't[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'` the regex `\[.*?\](?=::|\s|$)` finds no `]` followed by `::`/whitespace/EOS, so it falls through to `bare.split('[', 1)[0]`, yielding `['t']` — `_unresolved_tests` still only verifies `tests/a.py::t` and never resolves `tests/missing.py::t2`, i.e. the invalid regression test is still accepted.

chunk_findings.detail: The test that is supposed to guard the intent's fix cannot fail on the unfixed code. Its input `"tests/a.py::t[a],tests/b.py::u[x]]"` puts the comma at bracket depth 0: `[a]` opens and closes before the comma, so even the unclamped `depth += {'[':1,']':-1}` splitter still hits depth 0 at that comma and returns the two expected entries. The negative-depth condition the bug is about (a `]` inside the id *before* the comma, as in `t[x]y],...`) never occurs here — the extra `]` in `u[x]]` sits after the comma and can only affect a later comma, of which there is none. A regression test that actually fails on the unfixed code needs the comma met while depth is already negative, e.g. `"tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/b.py::u"`, which the added test does not do, so `ddflow complete ... --regression-test` would close the bug on a test that passes either way.

chunk_findings.detail:
The change does not fix the bug it is attached to. The intent says the defect is that `_split_outside_brackets` does `depth += {'[':1,']':-1}` without clamping, so a `]` inside a parametrize id drives depth negative and a following comma is never treated as a separator. But this diff modifies only `_bare_names`; `_split_outside_brackets` is untouched and its depth arithmetic still goes negative.

Concretely, with the exact probe input from the intent, after this change `_split_outside_brackets('tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2')` still returns the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2']` (the `]` after `y` puts depth at -1, so the comma is considered "inside brackets"). `_unresolved_tests` therefore still never receives `tests/missing.py::t2` as a separate entry, and a missing regression test is still accepted — the reported bug is unaddressed.

The new `_bare_names` filter cannot compensate. Applied to that glued entry it removes `[x]`, yielding parts `['tests/a.py', 'ty],tests/missing.py', 't2']`; the filter drops every part containing `]`, so the middle part is discarded and the result is `['tests/a.py', 't2']`. The `tests/missing.py` file path is gone entirely, so nothing downstream inspects it. Fixing `_bare_names` only suppresses a phantom *name*; it never restores the *split* the bug is about.

chunk_findings.detail:
Given `spec = "tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"` (a real parametrize id `[a],b`, i.e. the inner list `[a]` plus a comma, wrapped by pytest's outer `[...]`):

- Trace of the new code: `[` → `inside=True`; `[` → `inside=True`; `]` with `after=","` → `inside = not True = False`; then `,` is seen while `not inside` → the string is split at the comma; the trailing `]` is ignored because `inside` is already `False`.
- Actual result: `["tests/a.py::t[[a]", "b]"]` — one node id became two fragments.
- Correct result (and what the *removed* clamped code produced): `["tests/a.py::t[[a],b]"]`. Under the old code `[[` drove `depth` to 2, the interior `]` decremented it to 1 (still > 0), so the comma inside the brackets did not split; the final `]` closed it correctly.

So this change regresses inputs that the clamped version handled. The comma here is inside the outer bracket, so `_unresolved_tests` will now receive the bogus fragment `tests/a.py::t[[a]` and fail to match the actual test — the same class of failure (a valid entry not resolved / a non-existent test reported) that Bfc9daca269 is about. The same happens for an interior `]` followed by whitespace, e.g. `"tests/a.py::t[[a] b,c]"` → `["tests/a.py::t[[a] b", "c]"]`.

The added test only exercises interior `]` followed by `]` (`t[[1]]`) or by a non-separator, so it never hits the `after in ",;" or after.isspace()` path on an interior bracket that still has a matching `]` later.
chunk_findings.title: `_split_outside_brackets` (ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py, the `elif ch == "]" and inside:` branch, ~line 80–86)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic only splits a bracketed entry when the text following the separator never makes the bracket depth negative, and `_closes_unopened` scans the *entire remaining string* — including later entries. A later entry whose parametrize id itself contains an unmatched `]` therefore cancels an otherwise legitimate split, merging the whole list into one entry. This is exactly the shape the module documents/test as valid (`t[a],b]`, `t[x]y]`) and it reproduces bug Bfc9daca269.

Concretely, `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d],e]")`:

- at the comma after `t[a]`, `cur` ends in `]`, but `_closes_unopened("b],tests/c.py::d],e]")` hits the `]` after `b` and returns True → no split;
- at the comma after `t[a],b]`, `cur` ends in `]`, but `_closes_unopened("tests/c.py::d],e]")` hits the `]` after `d` and returns True → no split again.

Result: `["tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d],e]"]` (one entry), whereas the correct answer is `["tests/a.py::t[a],b]", "tests/c.py::d],e]"]`. The pre-change code split here, because `_NEXT_PATH` matched `tests/c.py` after the second comma, so this is a behavioral regression introduced by the change, not a pre-existing limitation. Note the added test `("tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/c.py::d[e]", ...)` deliberately uses a *balanced* second id (`d[e]`), which is why it passes; the `d],e]` variant (a value holding `]` and `,`, explicitly listed as supported in the docstring) fails. The same root cause also blocks a split when a command following a bracketed id contains a `]` (e.g. `tests/a.py::t[x], pytest -k "a]b"`).

Because the missing second node id is never separated, `_unresolved_tests` again evaluates it as part of the first token, so a nonexistent regression test can be accepted — the very failure Bfc9daca269 intends to fix.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `_NEXT_PATH` disjunct is OR-ed ahead of the `_closes_unopened` guard, so a `.py`-looking token after a `]` forces a split even when the rest closes a bracket the entry never opened (i.e. even when the comma is provably inside a parametrize id, the case `_closes_unopened` exists to protect). Input:

    _split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b.py,c]")

At the first comma `cur` is `tests/a.py::t[a]` (ends with `]`) and the rest is `b.py,c]`; `_NEXT_PATH` matches `b.py` because `.py` is followed by `,` (in the `[\s,;]` lookahead). So it splits, `bracketed` resets to `False`, and the second comma splits again via the `not bracketed` branch, yielding three entries `["tests/a.py::t[a]", "b.py", "c]"]`. The docstring this diff touches explicitly promises that a parametrize value may hold `]` and `,` (`t[a],b]` is one value); the old condition kept this as the single entry `tests/a.py::t[a],b.py,c]` because `_closes_unopened("b.py,c]")` is true and blocks the split. So a single bracketed id whose value contains a `.py` token followed by a separator is now shredded into spurious "test" entries, which then feed `_unresolved_tests` — exactly the failure class (wrong number of parsed tests) the change is meant to eliminate. The added regression cases all place the `.py` path after a separator that is *between* entries, so they do not cover this shape; e.g. `tests/a.py::t[a],b.py::c]` (rest `b.py::c]`) also matches `_NEXT_PATH` and splits a single id.

chunk_findings.detail: `_PARAMS = re.compile(r"\[.*?\](?=::|\s|$)", re.S)` ends a parametrize id at the *nearest* `]` that is followed by `::`, whitespace or end-of-string. That lookahead is exactly the invariant B-bfu-param-sep documents as legal content inside an id ("`::` and `,` are legal inside `[...]`"). When an id contains `]` immediately before `::`, the regex mistakes the interior `]` for the id's terminator and strips only part of the id. Concrete input: `_bare_names("TestC::test_m[x]::y]")` (a valid pytest node id for `tests/test_a.py::TestC::test_m` parametrized with `ids=["x]::y"]`). The regex matches `[x]` (the `]` is followed by `::`), so `_PARAMS.sub` yields `"TestC::test_m::y]"`, and the function returns `['TestC', 'test_m', 'y]']` instead of the documented `['TestC', 'test_m']` — a spurious name `y]` is emitted that no test defines, so `_unresolved_tests` will treat a legitimate node id as unresolved/missing. This is a regression introduced by the change: the previous `names.split("[", 1)[0].split("::")` cut at the first `[` and produced `['TestC', 'test_m']` here, i.e. accepted the same id. The function's own docstring promises "every parametrize id removed", which this input violates.

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug Bfc9daca269 lives in `_split_outside_brackets`, which per the intent does `depth += {'[':1, ']':-1}` without clamping, so the probe `_split_outside_brackets('tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2')` returns a single entry. This diff never edits `_split_outside_brackets`; it only rewrites `_bare_names` (and its docstring). Consequently the behavior called out as buggy is unchanged: after this change the comma-joined string is still split into one entry, `_unresolved_tests` still only sees `tests/a.py::t...`, and `tests/missing.py::t2` is still never resolved. The new test in `tests/test_regression_test_split.py` asserts only `_bare_names(...)` results (and two of its four assertions, `TestC[1]::test_m` and `[p]`, already pass on the unfixed code), so it neither reproduces Bfc9daca269 nor fails when `_split_outside_brackets` remains unclamped. The regex matches `[x]` (the `]` is followed by `::`), so `_PARAMS.sub` yields `"TestC::test_m::y]"`, and the function returns `['TestC', 'test_m', 'y]']` instead of the documented `['TestC', 'test_m']` — a spurious name `y]` is emitted that no test defines, so `_unresolved_tests` will treat a legitimate node id as unresolved/missing. This is a regression introduced by the change: the previous `names.split("[", 1)[0].split("::")` cut at the first `[` and produced `['TestC', 'test_m']` here, i.e. accepted the same id. The function's own docstring promises "every parametrize id removed", which this input violates.

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug Bfc9daca269 lives in `_split_outside_brackets`, which per the intent does `depth += {'[':1, ']':-1}` without clamping, so the probe `_split_outside_brackets('tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2')` returns a single entry. This diff never edits `_split_outside_brackets`; it only rewrites `_bare_names` (and its docstring). Consequently the behavior called out as buggy is unchanged: after this change the comma-joined string is still split into one entry, `_unresolved_tests` still only sees `tests/a.py::t...`, and `tests/missing.py::t2` is still never resolved. The new test in `tests/test_regression_test_split.py` asserts only `_bare_names(...)` results (and two of its four assertions, `TestC[1]::test_m` and `[p]`, already pass on the unfixed code), so it neither reproduces Bfc9daca269 nor fails when `_split_outside_brackets` remains unclamped. If the intended fix is the clamp on the bracket depth, the wrong function was modified and the reported bug remains reproducible.

chunk_findings.detail: The change does not touch the function the bug report (intent) identifies as the cause. The intent states bug Bfc9daca269 is that `api/knowledge/regression._split_outside_brackets` does `depth += {'[':1,']':-1}` without clamping (unlike `_looks_like_several`, which clamps with `max(0, ...)`), so for the input `'tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'` it returns a single entry and the second test is never checked. The diff only edits `_PARAMS`/`_PARAMS_LOOSE` and the body of `_bare_names`; `_split_outside_brackets` is not in the diff at all (part 1 of 1). Comma-splitting is character-by-character bracket-depth logic and does not call `_PARAMS` or `_bare_names`, so the new regex cannot change how many entries the split produces. Concretely, with the patched code `_split_outside_brackets('tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2')` still yields `['tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2']`, `_bare_names` on the mangled tail `t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2` still returns `['t']` (neither `_PARAMS` nor `_PARAMS_LOOSE` matches, since the only `]` is followed by `y`), and `_unresolved_tests` therefore still checks only `tests/a.py::t`, so `tests/missing.py::t2` remains unresolved. The regression test added here (`test_a_missing_method_after_a_spaced_class_value_is_reported`, using `tests/test_a.py::TestC[a] b]::test_m_missing`) exercises the `_bare_names` path and does pass with the patch, but it is a different symptom than the reported bug: the missing depth clamp is never fixed.
