chunk_findings.detail: The clamp fixes the reported direction (a trailing `]` after the id's closing `]` made depth negative and swallowed the following separator) but trades it for the opposite failure for any single node id whose param value contains two `]` and then a comma inside the id's brackets. `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]")` — the node id for `@pytest.mark.parametrize("s", ["a]b]c,d"])` — traces as: `[`→1, `]`→0, second `]`→`max(0,-1)=0`, then `,` is seen at depth 0 and splits, returning `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c", "d]"]`. Under the old code the second `]` drove depth to -1, so the `,` was kept and the function returned the single entry `["tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]"]` — which is the correct parse (the comma is inside the id's brackets). The clamped version therefore rejects a regression test that actually exists: `_unresolved_tests` will check `tests/a.py::test[a]b]c` and `d]`, find neither, and report the valid node id as missing. This is the mirror image of the bug being fixed, so the `max(0, ...)` heuristic is only sound when the deeper `]` is the id's final character; it needs the same treatment its sibling `_looks_like_several` gets or a bracket-count that is not reset by an in-value `]`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py `_split_outside_brackets` (the `depth = max(0, ...)` line)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new heuristic decides a `]` closes the parametrize id's brackets whenever the next character is `""`, `,`, `;` or whitespace. But the whole reason for this bug is that a parametrize value may itself contain `]`, and such a value may also contain `,`/`;` (the sibling test `tests/a.py::t[1,2;3]` already asserts commas/semicolons inside brackets must not split). When the embedded `]` is immediately followed by a separator, the code wrongly treats it as the closing bracket.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b]")`. Tracing line 86-88: at `[`, `inside=True`; the `a` is appended; at the first `]`, `spec[i+1]` is `','`, so `after in ",;"` is true and `inside` is set to `False`; the following `,` then hits `if ch in ",;" and not inside` and splits. The call returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]']` (and the two-entry list `"tests/a.py::t[a],b],tests/b.py::u"` returns three entries `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b]', 'tests/b.py::u']`) instead of the single entry `tests/a.py::t[a],b]`. This is structurally identical to the case the new test covers (`tests/a.py::test[a]b]c,d]`, where the embedded `]` happens to be followed by `b` rather than the comma): one `[`, two `]`, comma between them; the outcome flips purely on the character after the first `]`, so `t[a],b]` is split inside its own brackets while `t[a]b]c,d]` is not. A value like `t[a] b,c]` (embedded `]` followed by whitespace then a comma) fails the same way via `after.isspace()`. The result is a spurious extra entry (e.g. `b]`) that `_unresolved_tests` will see as a missing test, i.e. the same "missing test never resolved / wrong resolution" failure mode this change was meant to eliminate.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:86-88 (`_split_outside_brackets`)

chunk_findings.detail: Over-split: any bracketed parametrize value containing a comma followed by a token ending in `.py` is torn apart, even though the comma is inside the id's brackets. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]")`: after `[` `bracketed=True`, every `,`/`;` is tested against `_NEXT_PATH.match(spec, i+1)`; at the comma the remainder is `b.py]`, which the regex matches (`[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` matches `.py`, `(?![\w.])` sees `]`), so it splits. The function returns `['tests/a.py::t[a]', 'b.py]']` instead of the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[a],b.py]']`. This is exactly the case the new test `test_a_value_whose_inner_bracket_meets_a_separator_stays_one_entry` covers for `t[a],b]` — it only passes because `b]` lacks the `.py`; the sibling input `t[a.py,b.py]` fails the same way (returns `['tests/a.py::t[a.py', 'b.py]']`). The pre-change code (comma suppressed while `inside`) returned one entry here, so this is a regression introduced by the diff, and the new tests do not exercise a value token ending in `.py`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:_split_outside_brackets (`_NEXT_PATH` + `bracketed` condition)

chunk_findings.detail: Under-split: once an entry is bracketed, a following separator is ignored unless the next entry starts with a file path, so a legitimate non-path entry is merged. Trace `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x")`: at the comma `bracketed=True` and the remainder ` pytest -k x` contains no `.py`, so no split; the result is the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[1], pytest -k x']`. The function's own contract ("entries separated by ',' or ';'") and the newly added `test_entries_without_brackets_split_as_before` treat `pytest -k x` as a separate entry (it splits there only because no `[` preceded it), so the behavior is inconsistent and the command is swallowed into the node id, which is the same failure mode (an entry that is never seen as its own item) that this change set out to fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:_split_outside_brackets (`_NEXT_PATH` + `bracketed` condition)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_closes_unopened` scans the *entire* remainder `spec[i+1:]`, which includes the following entries, so an unbalanced `]` inside the *second* entry's parametrize value is misread as "closing a bracket the current entry never opened", and the split is suppressed.

Concrete input: `_split_outside_brackets("tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]")`.

- At the comma, `cur == "tests/a.py::t[x]"` ends with `]` (first condition passes).
- `rest == "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"`. Walking it: `[` → depth 1, the first `]` → depth 0, then the trailing `]` → depth −1, so `_closes_unopened` returns `True`.
- The `and not _closes_unopened(...)` term is therefore `False`, the separator is appended to `cur`, and the function returns the single entry `["tests/a.py::t[x],tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]` instead of the two entries `["tests/a.py::t[x]", "tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]"]`.

The docstring itself declares `t[x]y]` a legitimate parametrize id, so `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is a valid second entry (its value is `a]b`). Because the list is not split, `_unresolved_tests` only looks at `tests/a.py::t` and the genuinely missing `tests/missing.py::t2[a]b]` is never flagged — precisely the failure mode Bfc9daca269 is supposed to close, still reachable whenever the second bracketed entry's value contains a `]`. The added test only covers a second entry with balanced brackets (`tests/c.py::d[e]`), so it does not exercise this case.

Note this is a regression relative to the removed `_NEXT_PATH` approach, which matched the second entry by its leading `… .py` token and split correctly here.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py (_split_outside_brackets / _closes_unopened)

chunk_findings.detail:
Input: `tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]`.

This is a single node id whose value is `a],b.py,c` (the documented shape `t[a],b]` generalised, i.e. the separator before `]` is inside the id, and the rest `b.py,c]` closes a `]` it never opened). On the *old* code the first comma sees `cur == "tests/x.py::t[a]"` (ends with `]`), and `_closes_unopened("b.py,c]")` is `True`, so the branch is not taken and the spec is correctly kept as one entry.

On the *new* code `_NEXT_PATH.match("b.py,c]", 0)` succeeds: `[\w./-]+` backtracks to `b`, `\.py` consumes `.py`, and the lookahead `(?=::|[\s,;]|$)` matches the following `,`. So the entry is split at the first comma, `bracketed` is reset to `False`, and the remaining comma (now "outside brackets") splits again. The function returns three entries:

    ["tests/x.py::t[a]", "b.py", "c]"]   # after
    ["tests/x.py::t[a],b.py,c]"]         # before (correct)

`b.py` here is a fragment of the parametrize value, not a following test path, so `_unresolved_tests` now resolves bogus entries (`b.py`, `c]`) instead of the real one. The asymmetry is visible in the regex's own comment: `t[a],b.py]` is handled (the `]` is not in the lookahead set), but `t[a],b.py,c]` / `t[a],b.py::c]` are not — the new "a test path follows" reason overrides `_closes_unopened` even when the following `.py` token is a value rather than an entry.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py:_split_outside_brackets (the `_NEXT_PATH.match(...) or ...` clause)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_malformed` encodes the assumption "a node id's parametrize part is its LAST part", so it flags any entry that contains `[` but does not end in `]`. Pytest node ids violate this for class-level parametrization: a class decorated with `pytest.mark.parametrize` produces ids of the form `tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m` (the parametrize bracket sits on the class, followed by `::method`), so such an id is a *valid, well-formed* node id but `_malformed` returns `True` for it. This makes the global minimum prefer merging a list that should split. Concretely, for

    spec = "tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m,tests/b.py::test_n[y]"

the only separator is the comma. Cutting there gives entries `"tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m"` (flagged malformed → 1) and `"tests/b.py::test_n[y]"` (valid → 0), i.e. `(1, -2, …)`. Not cutting gives the single entry `"tests/a.py::TestC[x]::test_m,tests/b.py::test_n[y]"`, which ends in `]` with `[` before it, so it is *not* flagged, i.e. `(0, -1, …)`. The `min` picks the fewer-malformed single entry, so `_split_outside_brackets` returns one entry even though there are two perfectly well-formed readings — directly violating the design's own rule that a genuinely ambiguous, well-formed input must resolve to *more* entries. The second test is then never checked on its own, which is the same failure mode the change was supposed to fix for `'tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'`; it just moves the trigger to any list whose first element is a class-parametrized node id and whose second element ends in `]`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py: `_malformed` / `_split_outside_brackets`

chunk_findings.detail: The new first clause exempts *any* piece that contains whitespace and doesn't itself start with a `....py::` path, which is broader than “a command”: a whitespace can also live inside a node id's parametrize value. Given `spec = "tests/a.py::t[a],hello world]"` — a single valid node id for a string parameter whose id is `a],hello world` (pytest keeps spaces in string ids; `_split_outside_brackets` is documented to handle params holding `]`, `[`, `,`, `;`, and space is no different) — the whole entry ends in `]` so `_malformed(whole)` is False, and the cut at the comma yields pieces `tests/a.py::t[a]` (well formed) and `hello world]`, which is also reported not malformed precisely because of the new whitespace clause. Both readings therefore have zero malformed entries, and the tie-break documented in the changed docstring (“the one with more entries wins”) makes `_split_outside_brackets` return `["tests/a.py::t[a]", "hello world]"]` — it splits one existing test id into a truncated id plus the garbage fragment `hello world]`. Before this change the old `_malformed` flagged `hello world]` (`]` with no `[`) as malformed, so the whole string was kept as a single well-formed entry and the real node id was resolvable; the added whitespace exemption is what introduces the wrong split, so a valid regression test is now reported unresolved (or a bogus `hello world]` test is looked up).

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug (Bfc9daca269) lives in `_split_outside_brackets`, and that function is never touched by this diff — the only production hunks are in `_unresolved_tests` and the new `_bare_names`/`_PARAMS`. So the probe from the intent still fails: `_split_outside_brackets('tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2')` sees depth 1 at `[`, back to 0 at the `]` after `x`, still 0 through `y`, then `]` drives it to −1; the following comma is at depth −1, not 0, so no split happens and the call still returns the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2']`. The new `_bare_names` does not compensate: for `names = 't[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'` the regex `\[.*?\](?=::|\s|$)` finds no `]` followed by `::`/whitespace/EOS, so it falls through to `bare.split('[', 1)[0]`, yielding `['t']` — `_unresolved_tests` still only verifies `tests/a.py::t` and never resolves `tests/missing.py::t2`, i.e. the invalid regression test is still accepted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py::_split_outside_brackets

chunk_findings.detail: The test that is supposed to guard the intent's fix cannot fail on the unfixed code. Its input `"tests/a.py::t[a],tests/b.py::u[x]]"` puts the comma at bracket depth 0: `[a]` opens and closes before the comma, so even the unclamped `depth += {'[':1,']':-1}` splitter still hits depth 0 at that comma and returns the two expected entries. The negative-depth condition the bug is about (a `]` inside the id *before* the comma, as in `t[x]y],...`) never occurs here — the extra `]` in `u[x]]` sits after the comma and can only affect a later comma, of which there is none. A regression test that actually fails on the unfixed code needs the comma met while depth is already negative, e.g. `"tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/b.py::u"`, which the added test does not do, so `ddflow complete ... --regression-test` would close the bug on a test that passes either way.

chunk_findings.detail:
The change does not fix the bug it is attached to. The intent says the defect is that `_split_outside_brackets` does `depth += {'[':1,']':-1}` without clamping, so a `]` inside a parametrize id drives depth negative and a following comma is never treated as a separator. But this diff modifies only `_bare_names`; `_split_outside_brackets` is untouched and its depth arithmetic still goes negative.

Concretely, with the exact probe input from the intent, after this change `_split_outside_brackets('tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2')` still returns the single entry `['tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2']` (the `]` after `y` puts depth at -1, so the comma is considered "inside brackets"). `_unresolved_tests` therefore still never receives `tests/missing.py::t2` as a separate entry, and a missing regression test is still accepted — the reported bug is unaddressed.

The new `_bare_names` filter cannot compensate. Applied to that glued entry it removes `[x]`, yielding parts `['tests/a.py', 'ty],tests/missing.py', 't2']`; the filter drops every part containing `]`, so the middle part is discarded and the result is `['tests/a.py', 't2']`. The `tests/missing.py` file path is gone entirely, so nothing downstream inspects it. Fixing `_bare_names` only suppresses a phantom *name*; it never restores the *split* the bug is about.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py::_bare_names (diff touches `_bare_names`, not `_split_outside_brackets`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change reworks `_bare_names`'s regexes but never touches the function the bug report names as the culprit: `_split_outside_brackets`, which still does `depth += {'[': 1, ']': -1}` with no `max(0, ...)` clamp (unlike its sibling `_looks_like_several`). Because the diff does not alter that splitter, the reported probe still produces the failing behavior: for `'tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2'`, `[` raises `depth` to 1, the `]` in `t[x]` drops it back to 0, and the second `]` in `t[x]y]` drives it to -1. From then on no comma is seen at depth 0, so `_split_outside_brackets` yields ONE entry, `_bare_names` is only ever handed the `tests/a.py::t...` prefix, and `tests/missing.py::t2` is never checked — i.e. a nonexistent regression test is still accepted (exactly the accept-invalid bug Bfc9daca269 describes). The regression test added in this diff does not exercise that path: it feeds `_unresolved_tests` a single, comma-free id, `"tests/test_a.py::TestC[a] b]::test_m_missing"`, so it can pass green while the reported unbalanced-`]` / comma-splitting bug remains unfixed. Either `_split_outside_brackets` must be clamped (or replaced by a split that tracks the `]`-in-id case), or the change does not fix the stated bug.

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug (Bfc9daca269) is that `_split_outside_brackets` updates depth with `{'[': 1, ']': -1}` without clamping, so a stray `]` in a parametrize id drives depth negative and a following top-level comma is no longer recognized as a separator. The probe in the intent, `_split_outside_brackets('tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2')`, must return two entries. This patch contains no edit to `_split_outside_brackets` (the only changed lines are the import list in `__init__.py` and a deletion in `tests/test_module_splits.py`). Running the probe against the code after this diff still returns the single unsplit string `['tests/a.py::t[x]y],tests/missing.py::t2']`, `_unresolved_tests` still inspects only `tests/a.py::t`, and `fixed`/`invalid` still accept a regression test that does not exist. The bug is not fixed; the imports added are the exported-test-surface names, not the fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/regression.py `_split_outside_brackets`

chunk_findings.detail: The patch deletes `assert set(homes) <= set(DEFINED[pkg.__name__])`, which was the guard that every function/class actually defined in the package's modules is also present in the module's `DEFINED` registry. After this deletion, a module that defines `def foo()` but omits `foo` from `DEFINED` passes the test silently — `homes` will simply not contain the entry that would violate the subset check, and the only remaining assertion is about *duplicate* homes, not about missing registrations. Concretely, if `foo` is later moved into a new module without being added to `DEFINED[pkg.__name__]`, the test that previously failed now passes, so the registry used by the split-detection code can silently drift out of sync with the code. That is a loss of coverage, not a fix for the bracket-depth bug.

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `assert set(homes) <= set(DEFINED[pkg.__name__])` is deleted. chunk_findings.detail: The file's own header (line 2) states that `subprocess` "is imported only by ddflow.infra.proc and ddflow.infra.git", i.e. the `subprocess-home` contract has two owning modules, yet the `ignore_imports` list only contains `ddflow.infra.proc -> subprocess` (the single `# home` entry); there is no `ddflow.infra.git -> subprocess` entry anywhere in the list. If `ddflow.infra.git` does import `subprocess` — which is exactly what the header asserts, and which the old, passing `.importlinter` baseline must therefore have suppressed — then the joined config the guard test builds is missing that allowlist entry. Running import-linter against the joined config will then report `ddflow.infra.git -> subprocess` as a violation of the `subprocess-home` contract, so the guard that previously passed now fails (behaviour is not identical to the old `.importlinter`); conversely, if the header is wrong and git does not import subprocess, the file still contradicts itself. The missing home entry for the second named owner is the concrete divergence: header says two home modules, baseline provides one.

chunk_findings.detail: The rule (and this function's own docstring) says the second rung is *the nearest* directory below the test dir, and only if that misses does it fall to the file's name. The code instead emits one "directory alone" rung for **every** directory between the file and the nearest test directory: `rungs = [([name], dirs), *(([d], []) for d in dirs), ([name], [])]`. For a nested data file this changes the outcome. Take `tests/fixtures/mcp-schema/schema.json`: `_dirs_below_tests` returns `["mcp-schema", "fixtures"]` (nearest first). Suppose the test that actually reads it builds the sub-directory from a variable and spells only `"schema.json"` (the B20b7744905 case, name built at run time), and some other test spells the standalone token `fixtures` (e.g. it references `tests/fixtures/other/...`). Rung 1 misses (no `mcp-schema`/`fixtures` token in the reader). The code then tries `mcp-schema` (no hit) and then `fixtures`, hits the unrelated test on the very first token match, and `break`s — so it selects a test that never reads `schema.json` and never reaches the intended final rung `[name]`, which would have selected the real reader. Intended behavior (rung 2 = nearest dir only, then rung 3 = name) selects the reader. Since `fixtures` is spelled by almost any suite that has `tests/fixtures/...`, this over/under-selection triggers for every changed file nested more than one level under a test directory where no test names the immediate sub-directory.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/testselect.py:_data_readers (the `rungs` list)

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring promises the word is matched "not inside a longer name", but the lookbehind excludes `.` while the lookahead does not, so a bare name followed by a dotted suffix still matches. With `word = "schema.json"` the pattern is `(?<![\w.-])schema\.json(?![\w-])`; in the text `"fixtures/schema.json.orig"` the character after `schema.json` is `.`, which is not in `[\w-]`, so the negative lookahead succeeds and `_names` returns True. Consequently, when the changed data file is `tests/fixtures/schema.json`, a test that only reads the backup `tests/fixtures/schema.json.orig` is selected even though it cannot read the changed file, contradicting the stated "not inside a longer name" boundary (the mirror-image case `old_schema.json` is correctly rejected by the lookbehind, showing the asymmetry is unintentional).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/testselect.py:_names (the `(?![\w-])` lookahead)

chunk_findings.detail: The rung list builds a "directory alone" rung for *every* directory in `dirs`, not just the nearest one, contradicting the stated rule ("…; failing that, the nearest such directory; failing that, the file's name; stop at the first rung that hits") and the function's own docstring ("the nearest such directory alone"). Concretely, with tests living only under `tests/`, a change to `tests/fixtures/data/report.json` makes `_dirs_below_tests` return `["data", "fixtures"]`. If no test spells `data` but many tests spell `fixtures` (for their own, unrelated fixture files), rung 2 skips past the nearest directory, matches `fixtures`, and selects every such test — tests that never name `report.json` or its directory `data` and therefore cannot read the changed file. And because selection stops at the first hitting rung, a test that *does* read the file by its exact name (the intended last-resort name rung) is never reached. Under the stated rule the nearest directory failing should fall through to the file's name, not to a farther, generic ancestor directory.

chunk_findings.detail: The right-hand boundary is `(?![\w-])`, which omits `.`, while the left-hand boundary is `(?<![\w.-])`, which includes it. The helper therefore still matches a name as a prefix of a longer dotted name, contradicting its documented contract ("not inside a longer name"): `_names("tmp_path / 'LICENSE.txt'", "LICENSE")` returns True, as does `_names('"fixtures.json"', "fixtures")`. Given a changed data file `tests/fixtures/x.json` (whose nearest directory rung is `fixtures`), a test that only writes its own `fixtures.json` is selected as a reader of `x.json` even though it cannot read it. Excluding `.` on the right, as on the left, would remove these false positives.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own fixture states the invariant that a bare file name is not evidence a test reads that file — `tests/test_licence_writer.py` is described as "writes a COPYING of its own: the bare name is not evidence it reads this one". But the rule it is testing keeps a third rung, "failing that, the file's name", which does exactly what the comment says is invalid. The added test only observes `test_licence_writer` being skipped because `test_conformance` (which does read a COPYING) hits rung 1 first, so "stop at the first rung" masks the bug; the bare-name rung is never actually exercised. Concretely, give the rule a changed file whose directory nothing spells: add/modify `tests/other/COPYING` (no test source mentions `other`). Rung 1 fails (no source spells `COPYING` with `other`), rung 2 fails (nearest directory `other` is named by no test), so rung 3 matches `tests/test_licence_writer.py` on the bare string `"COPYING"` and selects it — a test that only writes its own COPYING and cannot read `tests/other/COPYING`. So the new rule still selects a test that cannot read the changed file, the failure mode the change's rationale claims to have eliminated.

chunk_findings.detail:
The rung list drops the final `([name], [])` fallback whenever `dirs` is non-empty, so a file below a test directory is only ever matched by "name + some directory" or by the nearest directory alone. A test that reads the file by spelling only its name (the directory coming from an imported constant) is now missed, even though the old code selected it. Concrete input: `changed = ["tests/fixtures/schema.json"]`, `tests = ["tests/test_reader.py"]`, with no test file living under `tests/fixtures`, so `dirs == ["fixtures"]` and `name == "schema.json"`. The test source is

```python
from conftest import FIXTURES
def test_r():
    (FIXTURES / "schema.json").read_text()
```

with `FIXTURES = Path(__file__).parent / "fixtures"` defined in `tests/conftest.py`. The test text contains `schema.json` but not `fixtures`, so rung 1 (`name` + one of `dirs`) fails, rung 2 (`dirs[0] == "fixtures"`) fails, and there is no longer a bare-name rung; the test that does read the file is not selected. The removed rung was exactly the "last resort" for paths assembled at run time, and the stated rationale for dropping name-alone ("a bare `LICENSE` or `.gitattributes` is also in tests that write one of their own") only justifies it for generic names, not for a specific name like `schema.json`; the implementation applies it to every nested file, so the narrowing is broader than its justification and produces a real false negative.

chunk_findings.detail: The "failing that, the file's NEAREST directory alone" rung is built from the first element of `dirs`, but `dirs` holds the directories between the test root and the file in path order (outermost first), so `dirs[0]` is the *farthest* directory, not the nearest. For a changed file `tests/fixtures/guard_baselines/case.json` with tests under `tests/`, `dirs == ["fixtures", "guard_baselines"]`, so the second rung tests for the word `fixtures`. Consequence: (a) the test that actually reads the file and spells only its immediate directory (`guard_baselines`) is never matched, because it does not spell the generic `fixtures` — e.g. `os.path.join(BASE, "guard_baselines", name)` with `BASE` defined as `"fixtures"` elsewhere selects nothing, whereas `dirs[-1]` would match; and (b) conversely every test that merely names `fixtures` (i.e. reads any fixture at all) is selected as a reader of `case.json`, which is exactly the over-broad match the new docstring says the nearest-directory rung exists to avoid ("a farther directory (`fixtures`) is in every test that reads any fixture at all"). The code therefore contradicts both its own docstring ("NEAREST") and the retained comment ("most specific first"); the rung must use the deepest directory (`dirs[-1]`), not `dirs[0]`.

Concrete input: `changed = ["tests/fixtures/schema.json"]`, `tests = ["tests/test_reader.py"]`, with no test file living under `tests/fixtures`, so `dirs == ["fixtures"]` and `name == "schema.json"`.
```python
from conftest import FIXTURES
def test_r():
    (FIXTURES / "schema.json").read_text()
```

The name‑alone rung is documented as the "last resort" that catches a test which builds the path from a directory constant (`FIXTURES / "corpus.jsonl"`), but it is unreachable whenever the file's NEAREST directory name also occurs in any unrelated test, because the preceding rung (`([dirs[0]], [])`) short‑circuits the loop.

Concretely, take a changed data file directly below a fixture directory: `tests/fixtures/corpus.jsonl`. For it `dirs == ["fixtures"]`, so the rungs are `(["corpus.jsonl"], ["fixtures"])`, `(["fixtures"], [])`, `(["corpus.jsonl"], [])`. Let the true reader be a test whose source contains `FIXTURES / "corpus.jsonl"` where `FIXTURES` is an imported constant; matching is case‑sensitive, so this test does not contain the lowercase token `fixtures` and therefore misses rung 1 (needs `corpus.jsonl` *and* a dir) and would only be caught by rung 3. But the change's own docstring states "`fixtures` is in every test that reads any fixture at all", so some other test (e.g. one containing `fixtures/other.txt`) matches rung 2; rung 2 is non‑empty, the loop records those hits and `break`s before evaluating rung 3, and the constant‑building reader is never selected.

So the input `tests/fixtures/corpus.jsonl` + reader `FIXTURES / "corpus.jsonl"` + any other test mentioning `fixtures` misses a test that does read the file — i.e. the newly added name‑alone rung fails to do the one thing it was added for in exactly the example given in the docstring. The same preemption happens for rung 1: if any test spells the file name together with the lowercased directory, the loop stops there and the constant reader is still missed.

chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/testselect.py:_names

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own fixture states the invariant that a bare file name is not evidence a test reads that file — `tests/test_licence_writer.py` is described as "writes a COPYING of its own: the bare name is not evidence it reads this one". But the rule it is testing keeps a third rung, "failing that, the file's name", which does exactly what the comment says is invalid. The added test only observes `test_licence_writer` being skipped because `test_conformance` (which does read a COPYING) hits rung 1 first, so "stop at the first rung" masks the bug; the bare-name rung is never actually exercised. Concretely, give the rule a changed file whose directory nothing spells: add/modify `tests/other/COPYING` (no test source mentions `other`). Rung 1 fails (no source spells `COPYING` with `other`), rung 2 fails (nearest directory `other` is named by no test), so rung 3 matches `tests/test_licence_writer.py` on the bare string `"COPYING"` and selects it — a test that only writes its own COPYING and cannot read `tests/other/COPYING`. So the new rule still selects a test that cannot read the changed file, the failure mode the change's rationale claims to have eliminated.

chunk_findings.title: tests/test_test_selection.py (the bare-name rung, exercised by the `test_licence_writer` fixture)

chunk_findings.detail: The "failing that, the file's NEAREST directory alone" rung is built from the first element of `dirs`, but `dirs` holds the directories between the test root and the file in path order (outermost first), so `dirs[0]` is the *farthest* directory, not the nearest. For a changed file `tests/fixtures/guard_baselines/case.json` with tests under `tests/`, `dirs == ["fixtures", "guard_baselines"]`, so the second rung tests for the word `fixtures`. Consequence: (a) the test that actually reads the file and spells only its immediate directory (`guard_baselines`) is never matched, because it does not spell the generic `fixtures` — e.g. `os.path.join(BASE, "guard_baselines", name)` with `BASE` defined as `"fixtures"` elsewhere selects nothing, whereas `dirs[-1]` would match; and (b) conversely every test that merely names `fixtures` (i.e. reads any fixture at all) is selected as a reader of `case.json`, which is exactly the over-broad match the new docstring says the nearest-directory rung exists to avoid ("a farther directory (`fixtures`) is in every test that reads any fixture at all"). The code therefore contradicts both its own docstring ("NEAREST") and the retained comment ("most specific first"); the rung must use the deepest directory (`dirs[-1]`), not `dirs[0]`.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/services/testselect.py` `_data_readers` (the `rungs =` line, ~new line 245)

chunk_findings.detail: The new last-resort "file's name alone" tier is a purely textual match, so it cannot tell a test that builds the *right* directory from a constant apart from a test that mentions the same basename in an unrelated context. Concrete input: change `tests/fixtures/sets/corpus.jsonl`, and add a test file `tests/test_other_corpus.py` whose source is `C = FIXTURES / "other" / "corpus.jsonl"` (it reads `tests/fixtures/other/corpus.jsonl`, a different file). The file's own directories below `tests` are `fixtures/sets` and `sets`, and the test spells neither, nor does it spell the nearest directory `sets`; so the selection falls through to the name-alone tier and returns `{"tests/test_other_corpus.py": "names data file tests/fixtures/sets/corpus.jsonl"}` even though that test never opens the changed file. The same holds for a test that *writes* its own file, e.g. `(tmp_path / "corpus.jsonl").write_text(...)` — the old docstring even called this out ("a bare file name is in every test that writes one of its own"), and the new docstring's claim that the picked test "still reads the file" is not something the name-only rule can establish. This is a false positive in exactly the direction the task asks about: a test is selected that cannot read the changed file.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_test_selection.py:331 (test_a_file_named_alone_is_the_last_resort)

chunk_findings.detail:
The fallback that catches a reader with a run‑time‑built part is gated on the specific rung being empty (`if not hit:`), so any single test that spells the file's name together with one of its directories suppresses the fallback for the whole file and hides every reader whose only spelled-out part is the name (or the nearest directory). The module docstring names exactly such readers (`FIXTURES / "corpus.jsonl"`, `BASELINES / f"{kind}.toml"`) as what the union exists to catch; the code only catches them when no other test spells name+directory.

Demonstration: changed file `tests/fixtures/mcp-schema/LICENSE`. `tests/test_precise.py` contains the literal `"fixtures/mcp-schema/LICENSE"`; `tests/test_constant.py` does `SCHEMA / "LICENSE"` where `SCHEMA` comes from a shared constant, so it spells `LICENSE` but no directory that appears in `dirs`. The first rung returns `[test_precise]` (non‑empty), `if not hit` is false, and `test_constant` — a genuine reader of the changed file — is never added to `out`, so a change to `LICENSE` runs only `test_precise` and the breakage `test_constant` would show is deferred to the gate. The same holds for the `BASELINES / f"{kind}.toml"` shape: once any test spells `guard_baselines/alpha.toml`, the reader that only names `guard_baselines` is dropped before the `names(t, dirs[0])` branch can be evaluated.
